text:
Haitian residents in Ohio reported to an ICE office after a Supreme Court ruling allowed the end of their legal immigration status.

Some individuals who reported to the Cincinnati office were fitted with ankle monitors.

Advocates and protestors gathered outside the ICE office to support the Haitian residents and oppose the policy change.

Several Haitian residents reported to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement office in suburban Cincinnati on Sunday, Aug. 2, and at least two people were given ankle monitors.

Many Haitians who reside in Ohio have received call-in letters from the Department of Homeland Security in the last two weeks after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling allowed the Trump administration to end their legal immigration status.

Between 7:30 a.m. and 11:30 a.m. Sunday, The Enquirer saw four people go into the ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations field office in Blue Ash for appointments and three people exit.

Samantha Searles, who works with Ignite Peace, a Cincinnati-based organization that advocates for peace and justice, said five or six Haitian residents entered the office as of 10 a.m. Searles said residents had received call-in letters for appointments until 2 p.m.

Philbert Viaud, a Haitian resident of Columbus, left the office with an ankle monitor. Viaud said ICE officials transferred his information to a field office near Columbus and told him to go there for an appointment on Aug. 12. He said he has been applying for asylum for the past four years.

Sony Prenice, a Haitian resident, told reporters she was given the option to either wear an ankle monitor or be deported with $2,600.

She chose the ankle monitor, which restricts her to a 75-mile radius around her address. To go beyond that, she must call ICE for permission.

Annette Huelskamp, who interpreted for Prenice, said Prenice is concerned about what the ankle monitor means for visiting her family in Indiana or in case of a medical emergency, as she is diabetic.

Carl Ruby, the senior pastor with Central Christian Church in Springfield, came to the office with a member of his congregation who was called in for an appointment.

Ruby waited outside the front entrance for his congregant to come back outside.

"I want the ICE agents to look out and see me praying," he said.

'You put my house on fire'

Viles Dorsainvil, executive director of the Haitian Community Help and Support Center in Springfield, said he saw the ankle monitors Haitian residents were given as reminiscent of chains and slavery.

"They don't want us to be here and now they try to put us in chains as if we did something wrong," he said.

Dorsainvil said he received a call recently from an American man asking Haitians to go back to their country and he tried to explain the effects of American policies in Haiti. He referenced the U.S. occupation of Haiti until 1934 and the constitution the U.S. forced on Haiti.

"The American people have to know that if we are here, it is because that the foreign policies of those big countries have failed our country and make it a hell for us," he said. "If you put my house on fire, you would have to expect that I would come to your yard."

What is temporary protected status?

The Trump administration ended temporary protected status, or TPS, in November 2025. Many of the estimated 15,000 Haitians living in Springfield were here under temporary protected status.

TPS is granted to immigrants from countries facing conditions such as natural disasters or armed conflict. The State Department continues to advise Americans against traveling to Haiti, citing "crime, terrorism, kidnapping, unrest and limited health care."

Miranda Hallett with the Miami Valley Immigration Coalition researches TPS as part of her work with the Human Rights Center at the University of Dayton. She said it's "cruel" to end TPS so abruptly, leaving Haitians in the United States with few paths to legal residency.

Hallett said the coalition has been providing legal aid to Haitians in Springfield for years. She said lawyers typically do not go to appointments with the ICE field office, but community volunteers are sometimes allowed in to witness. It's up to the discretion of the office, she said.

"People without secure status have been detained when they come to call-in appointments which is why it's so terrifying for people to lose TPS" she said.

Protestors line up outside ICE office

Roughly 550 people came to protest ICE, according to organizers with Ignite Peace.

Protesters held signs that said "Keep TPS," "Let Haitians Stay" and "Melt ICE." They sang "This Land Is Your Land" and applauded as people entered and exited the ICE field office.

name: Human Rights
title: New regulation puts foreign journalists and a free press at risk
authors: Margy O’Herron and Dan Berger, opinion contributors
description:
Under the new rule, journalists are required to re-apply every eight months, though the rule doesn’t offer clear standards for review.
The regulation also invites other countries to retaliate against American journalists abroad, as the labor union NewsGuild-CWA pointed out.
When the U.S. imposed restrictions on Chinese journalists in 2020 in the middle of the COVID-19 pandemic, China slowed visa processing for U.S. journalists operating there.
And in 2024, Russia banned 92 U.S. journalists from the country, contending it was retaliating for anti-Russian reporting.
If we believe in a free press, Congress must do more to allow journalists to do their critical work freely and safely.
text:
On July 17, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security issued a new regulation that dramatically restricts foreign reporters’ ability to work independently in the U.S. The new rule, which takes effect in 60 days, would enable the U.S. government to reward favored journalists and punish perceived opponents; invite other countries to retaliate against American reporters abroad; and signal broad distrust of the press at a time when journalists already face deadly targeting. Amid the Trump administration’s broader effort to restrict press freedoms here at home, Congress must step in to limit the damage.

The regulation cuts the length of journalist visas — known as I-visas (for the section of the law that authorizes them) — down to eight months. The previous unlimited time frame offered stability and predictability. Under the new rule, journalists are required to re-apply every eight months, though the rule doesn’t offer clear standards for review. This puts journalists in a fragile situation.

This latest move is one in a series of limitations on the press, including lawsuits against media outlets for unfavorable coverage, limiting press access at the Pentagon, and most recently subpoenas served on New York Times reporters for publishing information about security features of the new Air Force One gifted by Qatar.

The rule proposed last fall seemed to include journalist visas as an afterthought (for a review of the main parts of the regulation on student and exchange visas see this analysis by the Brookings Institution). And the administration cherry-picked data to argue that the number of I-visas granted each year has significantly increased since 1985 when the current rule was enacted. Only 12,924 I-visas were approved in 2024, less than the 16,753 the rule says were issued in 1985. There was no clear rationale offered for the changes to the I-visa.

The Department of Homeland Security received nearly 22,000 comments in response to the proposed rule, nearly all critical of the change.

For instance, the Writers Guild of America East, a labor union for journalists, noted that the regulation sets up bureaucratic hurdles that the government could use to reward journalists it approves of while punishing journalists it finds disagreeable. That amounts to censorship.

The concern is not theoretical. Over the last year, the U.S. government retaliated against at least two international journalists who wrote critically about the Trump administration. Mario Guevara, an Emmy award-winning reporter in Atlanta, was arrested last June by ICE after live-streaming commentary on a No Kings protest. He was deported to El Salvador after three months in ICE detention. And in March of this year, journalist Estefany Maria Rodriguez Florez was arrested, allegedly because of her reporting on ICE activities.

Those arrests run counter to the First Amendment’s guarantee of freedom of speech, which a court recently reiterated applies to citizens and noncitizens alike.

The regulation also invites other countries to retaliate against American journalists abroad, as the labor union NewsGuild-CWA pointed out. That has happened before. When the U.S. imposed restrictions on Chinese journalists in 2020 in the middle of the COVID-19 pandemic, China slowed visa processing for U.S. journalists operating there. And in 2024, Russia banned 92 U.S. journalists from the country, contending it was retaliating for anti-Russian reporting. Reporters Without Borders, an organization working to protect independent journalism, summed it up: “Maintaining fair and predictable visa procedures for foreign journalists is essential to protecting reciprocal treatment for American media professionals.”

Yet the regulation was finalized without sufficiently addressing any of those concerns.

More broadly, the rule signals the U.S. government’s distrust of journalists at a time when they face deadly targeting around the world. Sixty-seven journalists were killed last year, while 503 were detained, 135 were reported missing, and 20 were held hostage, according to Reporters Without Borders.

Congress must take action. Lawmakers should exercise their oversight authority and hold hearings on the rule’s likely effects on freedom of the press.

Congress should also pass legislation to stop the rule from taking effect and even expand protections for journalists. In 2021, in the wake of the murder of Washington Post reporter Jamal Khashoggi, Sens. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) and Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) co-sponsored the International Press Freedom Act, a strong bipartisan bill that included an expansion of the I-visa to include journalists threatened while working abroad. That bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee, but went no further. If we believe in a free press, Congress must do more to allow journalists to do their critical work freely and safely.

At a time when freedom of the press is under attack around the world, the U.S. increasingly risks being perceived as a repressive regime instead of an example to the world of what a free press can be. Congress can’t let that happen.

Margy O’Herron is a fellow in Cornell’s Migration and Human Rights Program and a senior fellow in the Liberty and National Security Program at the Brennan Center for Justice. Dan Berger is also a fellow in the Cornell program, and a partner at Green and Spiegel LLC leading the academic and medical immigration team.

title: Media shifts to more aggressively fight Trump in courts - The Hill
description:
So, watching them fight this is important,” said Lisa Zycherman, vice president of legal programs at the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press.
Trump himself explained the administration wasn’t specifically after the journalists, but rather the source of the information they reported.
When CBS moved to settle its legal fight with Trump, its parent company, Paramount, was in the process of merging with Skydance Media, a conglomerate owned by Trump ally Larry Ellison, as part of a deal that required clearance from Trump administration regulators.
The White House and Trump’s legal team declined to comment.
And these big media companies can see the proverbial light at the end of the tunnel,” one national republican strategist told The Hill this week.
text:
Several major media companies that have been targeted by litigation from President Trump and top administration officials are fighting back in court, signaling a new era of tension between the president and a press he and his allies view as overly hostile toward him.

The trend stands in contrast to a string of high-profile settlements and capitulations made by major media companies during the first year of Trump’s second term and could be a sign that more outlets are now willing to devote time and resources to defending themselves in court from the president’s claims.

Trump, in his personal capacity, has sued The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the BBC within the last year, and several of his top Cabinet secretaries have either threatened to or filed litigation against other media organizations, including The Atlantic and MS NOW.

Many of these outlets have pushed back forcefully on what they describe as frivolous litigation designed to crack down on the independent press and intimidate journalists.

“I don’t know so much if it’s a shift in posture as it is these media organizations putting the administration to their burden of proving an actual malice standard, which is a really strong protection. So, watching them fight this is important,” said Lisa Zycherman, vice president of legal programs at the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press.

“Governments can’t bring libel claims, so these sorts of lawsuits have really been against the norm and that seems to have been majorly disrupted [in the Trump era],” Zycherman said.

Trump’s suit against the Times, arguably the highest profile of any against a media outlet, stems from its coverage of his reelection bid, which the president’s attorneys argue defamed him.

Observers have pointed to the case as part of a broader pressure campaign carried out by the administration against the Times. Earlier this month, the Department of Justice (DOJ) subpoenaed Times reporters over the outlet’s stories on security issues surrounding a Qatari jet gifted to Trump to use as a new Air Force One.

After the Times pushed back against the subpoenas in court, the DOJ agreed to withdraw them.

Trump himself explained the administration wasn’t specifically after the journalists, but rather the source of the information they reported.

“We’re not after journalists. We’re after leakers,” he said in the Oval Office last week. “And the way you find them is through the journalists.”

“That person should be found, and the way you find them is to tell the journalist, if it’s something having to do with national security, you tell the journalist: ‘Who is it?'” he added.

Trump was also handed a separate legal defeat this past week in his lawsuit against the BBC, which he brought over the way it edited a story on a speech Trump gave just before the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.

A judge in that case ruled the president had to produce financial documents to the BBC from his trust, paving the way for the outlet to make the president prove it damaged him with the edit.

The Wall Street Journal, owned by conservative media tycoon Rupert Murdoch, also this week asked a federal judge to toss a defamation suit brought by Trump over its reporting on his ties to the late financier Jeffrey Epstein.

It all fits a new trend of media companies fighting back more forcefully against Trump’s legal claims, observers say, after some high-profile cases involving major broadcasters ended last year with the companies settling with Trump to end the litigation.

ABC paid the president more than $15 million to settle a defamation claim over false statements anchor George Stephanopoulos made on air, while CBS agreed to pay the president $16 million months later to quash a lawsuit he brought over the way it edited an interview with former Vice President Harris, which aired on “60 Minutes.”

In both cases, media critics at the time said the settlements would have the effect of weakening press freedoms.

When CBS moved to settle its legal fight with Trump, its parent company, Paramount, was in the process of merging with Skydance Media, a conglomerate owned by Trump ally Larry Ellison, as part of a deal that required clearance from Trump administration regulators.

The Paramount-Skydance deal was given the green light after the settlement was paid.

The White House and Trump’s legal team declined to comment.

Mark Feldstein, the Richard Eaton chair of broadcast journalism at the University of Maryland, argued that there’s a key difference between how television networks and print media have handled lawsuits from Trump.

“Television news has always been more timid than newspaper and magazine reporting and online reporting because it’s licensed by the federal government,” Feldstein said.

He suggested networks are more likely to settle because “the bigger expense was the unknown revenge of what Trump might do.”

Print and online media fight back, he said, because “their economics are a lot more precarious than broadcasters’ are. So, they can’t afford to pay these large multimillion-dollar settlements the way television networks can.”

The business and political realities are different today than during the early months of Trump’s second term, other voices say.

“Look, he has about two years left. And these big media companies can see the proverbial light at the end of the tunnel,” one national republican strategist told The Hill this week. “These lawsuits are designed to modify publisher behavior, but it looks like many of them sort of see this as a bit of a paper tiger of sorts.”

Feldstein echoed the strategist’s sentiment.

“As Trump’s power wanes, whether that’s because his term is coming to an end or for whatever reason … there’s going to be less and less of this because this is strictly a response to power,” he said.

title: ICE detentions set Trump-era high in July, as immigration crackdown widens - CBS News
description:
The over 46,000 book-ins in July surpassed the roughly 43,000 detentions recorded by ICE in June, at the time the highest tally during President Trump's second term.
As of this weekend, ICE was holding 68,000 detainees in its sprawling detention system, approaching a record high of over 70,000 detainees set in January, according to internal agency figures.
But the latest phase of the crackdown has reignited the country's debate over ICE and its tactics.
As of July 12, we have now deported over 985,000 illegal aliens and arrested over 1 million illegal aliens."
Now, Cardinal Brown noted, ICE is dramatically expanding enforcement without the same "in-your-face" approach as before.
text:
Detentions by Immigration and Customs Enforcement set a monthly record high for the second Trump administration in July, internal agency data obtained by CBS News shows, as ICE widened its crackdown, making arrests at airports, immigration check-in offices and communities across the U.S.

Last month, ICE took into custody more than 46,000 individuals facing deportation because of alleged immigration violations, like entering the U.S. illegally or overstaying their visas, according to preliminary Department of Homeland Security figures.

The statistics, which have not yet been publicly disclosed by the federal government, show that a summer enforcement surge by ICE continued to intensify in July, as the agency faced pressure from the White House to record 2,000 arrests across the country each day. An average of 1,500 detainees entered ICE custody each day last month, the data indicates, though some of them were first arrested by Customs and Border Protection agents.

The over 46,000 book-ins in July surpassed the roughly 43,000 detentions recorded by ICE in June, at the time the highest tally during President Trump's second term. As of this weekend, ICE was holding 68,000 detainees in its sprawling detention system, approaching a record high of over 70,000 detainees set in January, according to internal agency figures.

The numbers also show the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration has rebounded this summer, following a significant drop in arrests earlier this year after federal agents killed two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during an enforcement blitz in Minneapolis that garnered bipartisan criticism.

While the Trump administration has largely stopped the large-scale, sweeping immigration operations it conducted in several Democratic-led cities last year, ICE has managed to more quietly boost arrest levels in recent weeks, including through a crackdown at airports and traffic stops, and the deployment of newly hired agents across the country.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin replaced Kristi Noem this spring with the stated goal of keeping ICE out of the headlines, while simultaneously furthering Mr. Trump's promise of overseeing the largest deportation operation in American history.

But the latest phase of the crackdown has reignited the country's debate over ICE and its tactics. Last month, ICE officers in Texas and Maine, respectively, killed two immigrants, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, during attempted traffic stops, triggering local and national outcry.

The fatal shootings prompted ICE to pause most vehicle stops, but the moratorium was short-lived, with Mr. Trump intervening and overturning the pause just 24 hours later. Investigations into both killings continue at the federal and local levels.

Instances of ICE agents in plainclothes arresting people near gates and check-in counters at airports throughout the country have also sparked controversy in recent weeks, prompting angry bystanders to film the arrests, some of which have gone viral online. The arrests have been made possible by increased collaboration between ICE and the Transportation Security Administration, which has been providing agents information on noncitizen travelers, including those whose status has lapsed.

The Trump administration has additionally broadened the population eligible to be arrested and processed for deportation, mostly recently terminating the Temporary Protected Status of more than 300,000 Haitian migrants. According to officials and advocates, some Haitian migrants in Ohio have begun receiving notices to report to local ICE offices, sparking fears in communities like Springfield.

The Department of Homeland Security told CBS News in a statement: "In President Trump's first year back in office, more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the U.S. because of the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration including an estimated 2.2 million self-deportations. As of July 12, we have now deported over 985,000 illegal aliens and arrested over 1 million illegal aliens."

"We're turning up the heat on the streets," Mullin said in a press conference last month. "We're out there working harder than we've ever had because we've empowered our law enforcement to do their job."

Theresa Cardinal Brown, an immigration official at DHS during the Obama and Bush administrations, said one main difference in ICE's strategy since Noem was pushed aside is how operations are advertised. Under the "previous leadership," she said, "there was an intent to make the enforcement public, to do it publicly, to be seen doing it."

Now, Cardinal Brown noted, ICE is dramatically expanding enforcement without the same "in-your-face" approach as before.

But she said it's clear "the administration never gave up on its goal of mass deportations."

name: Human Rights
title: Asylum-seekers and kids in court are Trump's next deportation target - The Hill
authors: Sarah Mehta, opinion contributor, Sarah Mehta, opinion contributor
description:
On Tuesday, the Trump administration introduced a new rule that diverts people who are applying for asylum straight to deportation court.
The U.S. humanitarian protection system is not just collapsing.
Several years ago, I met a woman who begged U.S. border agents not to send her back to Guatemala, where she feared for her life.
With roughly 1.3 million people losing humanitarian protection and plans to detain asylum seekers and others overseas, it is only going to get worse.
On Friday, children faced the possibility of losing their lawyers and going through deportation alone, potentially to traffickers.
text:
On Tuesday, the Trump administration introduced a new rule that diverts people who are applying for asylum straight to deportation court. The new rule, which is being billed as an “efficiency” and went into effect immediately, is an attempt to multiply deportations by plucking people who applied for asylum out of an administrative line and dumping them into mass deportation hearings without time to prepare their cases.

The U.S. humanitarian protection system is not just collapsing. It is being systematically attacked from within by an administration that is willing to send people to be tortured in a foreign prison, detain children on a toxic former military base and end their legal representation and deport Iranian women to war zones while sharing their confidential case information on activists with the Iranian government.

But faced with the evidence that this administration is prepared to send people to their deaths, many politicians and commentators continue to push for policies that severely limit humanitarian protection. This is, at best, tone deaf in our current moment.

A new report from my organization, the American Civil Liberties Union, explains that rules limiting access to asylum by capping how many people can apply and where, or making the standard harder are expedient and arbitrary policies that do not update the asylum system or border processing. They are merely proposals to limit the number of people who can lawfully seek access to protection.

And right now, advancing restrictionist proposals — despite evidence of their past failure, and at a time when the Trump administration is attacking all lawful immigration — is not just lazy; it’s dangerous.

Several years ago, I met a woman who begged U.S. border agents not to send her back to Guatemala, where she feared for her life. But she was deported anyway. Once there, her son was murdered, and she was kidnapped and gang-raped by those who took her son.

When previous closed-border policies like Title 42 were in effect, numerous people were preyed upon by organized criminal gangs while they waited in Mexico for a chance to see safety. Human Rights First documented at least 13,480 reports of murder, torture, kidnapping, rape and other violent attacks on people stuck in Mexico while this policy was in effect.

Sacrificing these individuals to bring a pretense of order to the border is both callous and completely unresponsive to the need for durable solutions for border processing.

The constantly-recycled restriction policies have never addressed the main reason people come to the border — the lack of lawful pathways for people to reunite with family, seek work and get protection. Nor do they help the communities or industries who want immigrants to come here.

The reality is that people who flee tremendous violence are, yes, seeking protection, but they also do want and expect to support themselves and their families when they come to the United States. Indeed, these individuals have been contributing tens of billions to our economy while supporting their families.

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R), for example, has warned that the potential deportation of 10,000 Haitian residents from his state will not only separate families but create enormous harm to the local economy. Already, in cities like Miami and New York, once-vibrant neighborhoods like Little Haiti now sit unusually quiet, as fear keeps community members indoors, away from their jobs.

Americans are watching their neighbors disappear. Parents are forced to leave their children alone in the U.S. rather than expose them to violence, conflict and other dangers if deported. With roughly 1.3 million people losing humanitarian protection and plans to detain asylum seekers and others overseas, it is only going to get worse.

This is the moment for politicians to defend asylum and finally engage with policies that create a safe and humane border arrivals system. That means expanded durable pathways that include asylum, modernized processing at the border, support for and coordination with state and local communities receiving newly arrived immigrants and investments in courts to address the backlogs.

Rushing people into deportation tribunals and cutting off protection has never been defensible, nor has it created lasting solutions that meet U.S. legal commitments, community needs or economic interests.

And meanwhile, the risks are not speculative.

Just last week, a man deported to Guatemala and his wife — who self-deported to join him despite her pending asylum court date — were found shot dead in a field, their infant alive beside them. Hundreds of thousands of our neighbors are bracing for possible deportation to Haiti, where parts of the country have been reduced to a “kill zone” according to the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. On Friday, children faced the possibility of losing their lawyers and going through deportation alone, potentially to traffickers.

This isn’t the time to recycle cruel failed policies. We are hurtling towards a humanitarian catastrophe. We need Congress to act now to protect longtime residents facing deportation to danger, reject looming bills that would gut asylum and protections for kids, and finally, build lawful pathways that can actually fix our immigration system.

Sarah Mehta is deputy director of policy and government affairs for immigration at the American Civil Liberties Union.

text:
For the past couple of days, I have commuted to work between Europe and Africa. When an estimated 60,000 migrants arrived in Ceuta, Spain’s autonomous outpost on the northern tip of Africa, from Morocco this week, businesses shut their doors and all available beds quickly disappeared.

So, we have been staying in the mainland Spanish port city of Algeciras, taking the one-hour ferry to and from Ceuta.

A fellow commuter is Isabel Hossein, a port police officer in Algeciras whose home is Ceuta. “I have documents, so it’s easy for me,” she says. “Sometimes I cross the border to Morocco just for lunch. Why not? The food is good.”

Isabel says the mass influx of migrants on Wednesday and Thursday was overwhelming for the residents of Ceuta. “People were afraid; there were so many young men everywhere,” she said.

“I am half Christian, half Muslim, as many in Ceuta are. We live peacefully together. But the numbers this time were scary.”

It has got me thinking about the journeys we take. At Algeciras, hundreds of cars line up daily for the ferry to Tangier. Moroccans from all over Spain, and elsewhere in Europe, depart here to go home for the summer holidays.

I am told that on motorways in Spain up to 1,000km away, the word “Algeciras” appears in Arabic to ensure people find their way here. They, of course, have documents.

In Ceuta, on Saturday, I saw hundreds of young men making their way back to Morocco on foot, under the watchful, occasionally threatening, eye of the Spanish military.

The undocumented ones

Exhausted by the heat, 48 hours earlier, the men swam to the shores of Ceuta.

“For the good life, humanity, safety, and all the things you need,” Abdelmajid said.

There was none of that available when they arrived in Ceuta, just extreme heat, thirst and a very hostile reception.

Of the estimated 60,000 Moroccans who arrived in little more than 24 hours, 90 percent had returned to Morocco by Saturday night.

Several indicated by rotating their wrists they would simply try again. “They were told to come. I saw it on Instagram, ‘Go to Spain and get money, jobs,'” she said. “It’s all a game.”

Dozens died in the attempt to reach Ceuta, and on Saturday evening, police divers were still recovering bodies from the surrounding waters.

The Spanish government blames criminal gangs and traffickers. Opposition politicians blame the left-wing Spanish government’s immigration policies for the weekend’s events, some describing it as “an invasion”.

Zia Yusuf, a senior figure in the anti-immigration Reform UK party, turned up in Ceuta to join those from the right and far right trying to set their narrative for the events.

A long way to come for a bit of social media, but this was powerful stuff: in a crisp white shirt and surrounded by muscled minders, I watched Yusuf extract a few words from young men who spoke little English.

On his X account, he told his nearly 150,000 followers: “I am in Ceuta, the scene of the 60,000 strong invasion. Spain has effectively militarised its border. Already spoken to Moroccan men here who say they are trying to get to Britain. More to come.”

No one I spoke to said they were heading for Britain. Though I’ve no doubt if you posed the question to someone with a passing idea of what you were asking – “Would you like to go to Britain?” – the answer would likely be, “yes”.

For some, it no doubt is a game. But here in Ceuta, amid the detritus of flippers and rubber floating devices that litter the beaches this weekend, a game with tragic consequences.

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

Santa Clara County and state leaders are gearing up for legal battle to block a planned ICE facility in South County.

The lawsuit filed last month by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and county officials argues the federal government has illegally bypassed environmental laws, local zoning rules and other statutes in advancing the project just east of Gilroy. A hearing to consider plaintiff’s preliminary injunction seeking an immediate halt to construction work is set for Sept. 9 at San Jose’s federal courthouse.

Revelations about the planned facility, first reported by San José Spotlight in May, have sent shockwaves throughout the Bay Area. Planning documents suggest the facility will include enough detention space to hold 150 people, fueling concerns that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) may be preparing for more extensive operations in the region.

Opponents of the project, located on unincorporated county land at 7240 Holsclaw Road, view the lawsuit as the most promising avenue to block it. San José Spotlight reached out to legal experts for their perspectives on the lawsuit, and what to expect as court proceedings get underway in just over a month.

What’s in the case?

The lawsuit names the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), ICE and the property’s owner — an LLC belonging to development firm Elmwood Capital Group — as the defendants.

In making their case to block the project, state and county officials argued federal authorities have failed to conduct environmental reviews or consult with state and local authorities, as required by federal mandates laid out in the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the Administrative Procedure Act. They also said the facility violates zoning rules that reserve the property exclusively for agricultural uses.

DHS has not laid out a detailed response to the legal claims — and representatives have repeatedly said there are no plans to create a detention center at the location. The claim contradicts blueprints which bear the logos for ICE and DHS and outline an ICE facility with detainee processing areas, as well as interview and holding rooms.

Federal officials have agreed to temporarily pause construction and demolition work at the site — first observed in April — under a compromise agreement struck earlier this month between both parties.

What are the environmental concerns?

The 25-acre parcel likely contains hazardous materials due to its history of use for agricultural research, according to the complaint outlining the state and county’s case.

“There are three decades of documented leaks and spills on the Holsclaw Property from hazardous materials, including thiram, a toxic fungicide, along with releases into the property’s septic system of DNA extraction waste, ethidium bromide, calcium hypochlorite and acid-based chemical wash water,” the complaint reads.

Given the risk development work at the site poses to the surrounding ecosystem and the agricultural value of land, the injunction asserts NEPA requirements obligate the federal government to conduct an environmental review of the project before proceeding.

“If there is a potential issue, you at least have to investigate it,” Tseming Yang, an environmental law professor at Santa Clara University, told San José Spotlight. “You then have to analyze it and then describe it, and it has to be in the document.”

In addition, the complaint warns that the planned 20,0000 square-foot facility could overwhelm the area’s septic system, which was designed for much more limited use.

The property owner has previously asserted that any construction work conducted at the site is covered by federal exemptions, according to court documents.

Even if the court sides with plaintiffs on their environmental arguments, the decision would likely only delay the project until the government can make good on environmental review requirements, according to Yang, who previously served as an attorney in the Environment Division of the U.S. Department of Justice.

But that delay could be substantial, David Sloss, a constitutional and property law professor at Santa Clara University, said.

“NEPA can slow stuff down a long time,” Sloss told San José Spotlight. “They can hold it up probably until the Trump administration is no longer in office, and then it may become moot at that point.”

Can local rules bind the federal government?

The arguments around land use raise thorny questions about whether federal or local authority should prevail in this case.

The U.S. Constitution’s so-called Supremacy Clause means that whenever federal laws contradict state laws, the federal statutes win out. In this case, this constitutional provision may open the door for the federal government to argue that its prerogative to build a facility at this site supersedes local zoning rules.

But the legal questions get even trickier, because the lawsuit also asserts that the property owner, who is leasing the property to the federal government, is bound by a contract with the county to preserve the land for agricultural purposes.

“That contractual obligation should be binding on the federal government, unless there’s something in the lease agreement that exempts the federal government from that contractual obligation,” Sloss said.

What to look for as the case unfolds

Opponents of the facility have filed a number of amicus briefs laying out arguments in support of the lawsuit. That includes one brief filed July 27 by a coalition of more than two dozen Bay Area and Central Coast city and county governments arguing the planned facility would cause widespread economic and social harms.

But the legal terrain may be perilous for attorneys representing the county and state. Since taking office, President Donald Trump’s administration has launched a concerted effort to rollback environmental regulations, issuing a variety of executive orders that have weakened pollution standards that sought to limit environmental contamination from industrial operations and manufacture.

“The changes in the law that are being pushed by the administration, might change how the case is evaluated,” Yang said. “Courts have not been as friendly to some of the (environmental) challenges as we’ve seen.”

Contact Keith Menconi at keith@sanjosespotlight.com or @KeithMenconi on X.

text:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is facing a conservative backlash after reaffirming his opposition to amnesty in a social media post, with critics arguing the hardline message contradicted comments he made hours earlier during an immigration speech in Oklahoma.

Hours after speaking at the National Governors Association Summer Meeting in Oklahoma City, Mullin wrote on X: "NO amnesty for illegal aliens. Ever."

"We are a nation of laws," he wrote. "If you are illegally present in the United States of America—you will be detained and deported. Period."

The post did little to quell criticism from some conservatives, who argued it conflicted with remarks Mullin made earlier in the day.

RED STATE GOVERNOR PUMMELED ONLINE AFTER DEFYING TRUMP’S DEPORTATION ORDERS

"Why were you at the National Governors Association Summer Meeting today saying the exact opposite of what you are posting now?" one user wrote on X. "Did you suddenly radically change your mind about America's immigration policy in the past couple of hours? Or are you a liar?"

Former Border Patrol Chief Gregory Bovino also criticized Mullin's remarks, writing on X that "Voters asked for mass deportations. Clear demand. High priority. No ambiguity." He added, "The guy running DHS is making the case for 'immigration reform.' We've seen this script before."

In a separate post, Bovino wrote that Mullin had delivered "a masterclass in how to give terrible answers during a single interview" and argued, "Now you know why we're not getting mass deportations."

Conservative commentator Robby Starbuck also weighed in, calling Mullin's remarks "a total betrayal."

During the event, Mullin argued the U.S. needs immigration reform, distinguished between immigrants pursuing legal status and those who are not, and called for changes to some employment visa programs to address labor shortages.

"We haven't had actual immigration reform since 1959. There's a reason. It's political," Mullin said. "Do you really need immigration reform? Yes, you do."

BIDEN ADMINISTRATION FORCED A FALSE CHOICE ON AMERICANS ABOUT IMMIGRATION

Mullin also argued the country should modernize some employment visa programs.

"If we're looking to grow our economy, then we need to look at making more permanent solutions," he said, adding that "there's a way to utilize labor where we're not having the participation rate we need to... and we can plug those holes."

At the same time, Mullin repeatedly emphasized that immigration laws must be enforced.

Mullin added that immigrants who entered the country illegally or overstayed their visas without pursuing legal status could not expect relief.

"There's nothing I can do for you," he said.

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: San Diego court sought to intervene in independent oversight board, newly released records show
description:
Months before the San Diego Superior Court told the Juvenile Justice Commission that it was revoking its administrative support, court officials sought to rewrite the volunteer panel’s bylaws to weaken its authority, newly released documents show.
Among other changes, the court planned to stop the commission from advising state and local officials about juvenile court operations.
The independent oversight body is charged with monitoring the juvenile court and juvenile justice programs operated by the San Diego County Probation Department.
Even so, a rival legal opinion written by San Diego County’s top lawyer in 2015 reached a different conclusion.
San Diego County declined to comment on the commission’s latest disclosures.
text:
Months before the San Diego Superior Court told the Juvenile Justice Commission that it was revoking its administrative support, court officials sought to rewrite the volunteer panel’s bylaws to weaken its authority, newly released documents show.

Among other changes, the court planned to stop the commission from advising state and local officials about juvenile court operations. It also tried to keep the volunteer board from releasing public findings and promoting policies without the court’s permission.

The bylaw revisions were suggested to the Juvenile Justice Commission in January 2025, records show — seven months before Superior Court officials announced they were withdrawing funding and other administrative support from the commission.

Court officials say their move to withdraw support from the commission was aimed at preserving the court’s neutrality, given it routinely adjudicates legal cases involving young people who enter the juvenile justice system.

But commission Chair Caitlin Radigan said the court’s actions are interfering with the commission’s ability to provide independent oversight of the juvenile justice system, including of the court itself.

She released a trove of documents last week that detail the court’s decision to rewrite the bylaws and subsequently suspend its formal support of the commission, an independent oversight board that is mandated by state law.

The proposed revisions were not well received by Radigan or the commission at large.

“The farther we move away from connection to community and modeling to citizens what oversight and accountability looks like, the less we are able to achieve that mission of ‘acting as the public’s conscience,’” Radigan responded to the court in March 2025, records show.

The San Diego Union-Tribune reported two weeks ago that the Juvenile Justice Commission is in jeopardy of going out of business due to the Superior Court decision to withdraw support.

The independent oversight body is charged with monitoring the juvenile court and juvenile justice programs operated by the San Diego County Probation Department. It also inspects the county facilities that house juvenile offenders and produces reports on its findings.

The commission is now made up of 10 volunteers, including people who experienced the juvenile justice system themselves as youths. Much of its work is done confidentially, but its reports and other findings traditionally have been posted for the public and the youth-advocacy community.

The dispute between commissioners and court officials comes as the state Attorney General’s Office is investigating the San Diego County Probation Department for allegations of civil rights violations.

It also comes as the county is defending hundreds of civil lawsuits filed by former foster youth and juvenile hall detainees who say they were sexually assaulted while in custody years ago.

San Diego Superior Court officials stopped posting commission meeting materials and inspection reports on their website on July 1, leaving those who want to monitor the juvenile court, youth detention facilities, group homes or other programs in the dark.

Commissioners told the Union-Tribune last month that they planned to resign en masse next month, when the liability insurance policy that protects them from civil lawsuits is set to lapse.

“This is not primarily a dispute about the commission,” Radigan told the Union-Tribune. “It is a story about how a public institution exercised its authority over a legislatively created oversight body.

“The court made the decision,” she said. “The commission didn’t decide to create this controversy.”

Judge Michael S. Groch took over as the Superior Court presiding judge Jan. 1. He was not in charge when the court decided to stop providing staff and other services to the Juvenile Justice Commission, but he has not responded to requests to discuss the issues.

A court spokesperson said the commission rejected the proposed changes in June 2025, saying it needed to retain autonomy over reports and public statements. Commissioners also insisted on preserving their authority to publish findings without court approval and engage the public without “excessive gatekeeping,” spokesperson Emily Cox said by email.

“JJC would not accept the level of oversight the court considered necessary to ensure ethical compliance,” she said. “Without such oversight, materials posted on the court’s website or issued publicly could create the inaccurate impression that the court endorsed the JJC’s findings, recommendations or policy positions.”

Cox said the court would be jeopardizing its own ethical standards if it did not act.

“It also created potential liability exposure if inaccurate or defamatory material were published and, most importantly, risked the compromising of the court’s obligation to remain fair, neutral and impartial on policy issues subject to oversight by local government entities,” she said.

Independent oversight of juvenile courts and juvenile justice programs, generally run by county probation departments, is codified in state law.

But the Welfare and Institutions Code sections that govern the volunteer oversight boards gives California’s counties broad discretion in determining how to set up and administer the individual bodies.

In San Diego County, the Juvenile Justice Commission was operated as a county program until 2014, when the Superior Court agreed to take over the responsibility at the county’s request.

For the past dozen years, the court has hosted commission materials on its website, provided office and other support services and paid the cost of liability insurance that protects volunteer commissioners in case they are sued for service-related claims.

Cox said the Superior Court evaluated the status quo and came away convinced that the commission was legally an arm of San Diego County. It secured an independent legal opinion confirming its determination, she said.

“Based on the statutory framework and the court’s legal analysis, along with the legal analysis provided by the legal services office of the Judicial Council, the court concluded that JJC is a county entity,” she said.

Even so, a rival legal opinion written by San Diego County’s top lawyer in 2015 reached a different conclusion.

“For the reasons detailed below, I conclude that the JJC is an adjunct of the Superior Court of the state of California and that the county does not have the legal obligation to provide the JJC and/or its members with defense and indemnification in the event a civil action was filed,” then-County Counsel Thomas Montgomery wrote.

“While there may have been some indicia of an employment relationship many years ago, those factors no longer exist and full responsibility for the JJC rests with the state of California,” he said.

According to a recent report by the Children’s Advocacy Institute at the University of San Diego, there is little consistency across California about which entity — the courts or the county — should oversee the oversight boards.

“The law establishing how juvenile justice commissions should be governed and overseen is not explicitly clear,” the November 2025 analysis said. “Thus, it is difficult to ascertain whether any given commission … is actually operating in compliance with what the law intends.”

The Children’s Advocacy Institute study found that 17 of the state’s 58 counties operate juvenile justice commissions administered by the courts, while 22 are overseen by counties. Supervision of the commissions in 18 counties are unclear, it said.

One California county — Los Angeles — meets the state mandate by running a probation commission.

Nonetheless, researchers said legislators generally locate oversight authorities outside the control of the agencies being monitored, in order to avoid potential conflicts of interest.

“Civil grand juries, for example, have long been required to ‘inquire into the condition and management of the public prisons’ within counties,” the report said. “They are independent of the agencies they review and function under the auspices of the superior court.”

The work of the San Diego County Juvenile Justice Commission has already been curtailed by the dispute with the Superior Court.

Meeting agendas, board minutes and even the names of commissioners themselves are no longer available on the court website. The annual reports from facility inspections also are not visible to the public, although commissioners said they are working to find an alternative.

San Diego County declined to comment on the commission’s latest disclosures.

“There’s nothing new to add,” county spokesperson Tammy Glenn said by email. “Thanks for checking in.”

Last month, Glenn said county officials were working with the court to reach a new agreement.

text:
The American Civil Liberties Union and its state affiliates have filed 54 administrative claims against the federal government on behalf of people who allege they were harmed by federal immigration enforcement, launching what the organization says is one of its broadest coordinated legal efforts challenging ICE operations.

The claims, filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act, span 17 states and Washington, D.C., and represent the first legal step required before individuals can sue the federal government. The ACLU said the filings allege a pattern of misconduct by federal immigration agents, including excessive force, unlawful arrests, racial profiling, retaliation against people exercising their First Amendment rights and abuse while in detention.

Among the claims is one filed on behalf of Dr. Norma Bowe, a New Jersey nurse and Kean University professor who alleges she was assaulted by federal agents while providing medical care outside Delaney Hall, an immigration detention facility in Newark. Other claims involve U.S. citizens and legal residents who say they were wrongfully detained or subjected to aggressive enforcement actions despite having legal status.

“These are not isolated incidents,” the ACLU said in a press release announcing the coordinated filings, arguing the claims reflect a broader pattern of unlawful conduct by federal immigration authorities.

The Department of Homeland Security rejected the allegations, defending its immigration enforcement efforts and criticizing the ACLU’s characterization of federal operations. The agency said its officers are trained to enforce immigration laws while protecting public safety and complying with federal law.

The administrative claims do not themselves constitute lawsuits. Under federal law, agencies generally have an opportunity to review and respond before claimants can pursue litigation in court. If the claims are denied or remain unresolved after the statutory review period, the individuals may seek damages through federal lawsuits.

title: Pedro Sanchez jets off on holiday as migrants refuse to leave Ceuta - Yahoo
description:
Pedro Sánchez arrived at an official residence in Lanzarote for a two-week summer holiday with his wife on Saturday afternoon.
Meanwhile, migrants slept on beaches and hid in tunnels and bushes in Ceuta following an unprecedented incursion that has plunged Europe into crisis.
Carmen Fúnez, an MP for Spain's conservative People's Party (PP), said: "While Ceuta suffers, Sánchez is on vacation.
The authorities in Ceuta have put up to 200 refrigerated morgue spaces on standby, according to Spanish media.
But the presence of so many minors will complicate the Spanish authorities' attempts to send some of the remaining migrants back across the frontier.
text:
Credit: Anadolu via Reuters

Spain's prime minister faced a barrage of criticism after jetting off to the Canary Islands for a holiday as hundreds of migrants refused to leave the Spanish territory of Ceuta.

Pedro Sánchez arrived at an official residence in Lanzarote for a two-week summer holiday with his wife on Saturday afternoon.

Meanwhile, migrants slept on beaches and hid in tunnels and bushes in Ceuta following an unprecedented incursion that has plunged Europe into crisis.

Spanish authorities drove tens of thousands back across the border, but bodies were still being fished out of the sea on Sunday as many of those who crossed overwhelmed asylum centres.

The Spanish prime minister was accused of "denying reality" by opposition MPs as he left for his break.

He caused further anger after sharing a playlist of his favourite songs on social media. The summer soundtrack included Madonna's single I Feel So Free and tracks by Charli XCX and the Rolling Stones.

Carmen Fúnez, an MP for Spain's conservative People's Party (PP), said: "While Ceuta suffers, Sánchez is on vacation. There is nothing crueller than denying reality."

Scores of migrants remained in Ceuta on Sunday, days after as many as 60,000 stormed into the Spanish exclave in the biggest incursion in the history of the EU.

Despite claims by Spain that "almost everyone" who entered had been returned, some estimates suggested thousands remained.

There were also reports that people smugglers were taking migrants to the Spanish mainland on jet skis and motorboats, although it was not clear if this was from Ceuta or the Moroccan coastline.

While the vast majority of the migrants who swam or walked into the territory on the coast of North Africa returned to Moroccan soil, significant numbers vowed to stay in an attempt to claim asylum in Europe.

At least 75 migrants were believed to have died in the mass incursion, Spanish authorities told The Telegraph, with most drowning as they desperately swam from the Moroccan side of the border fence into the Spanish exclave.

Divers from Spain's Guardia Civil continued to scour the sea for bodies on Sunday, and the death toll is expected to rise. The authorities in Ceuta have put up to 200 refrigerated morgue spaces on standby, according to Spanish media.

In the biggest irregular border crossing in Ceuta's history, between 50,000 and 60,000 migrants from Morocco and sub-Saharan Africa stormed into Ceuta on Thursday and Friday, apparently with the connivance of the Moroccan authorities.

As the search for more bodies continued, some migrants chose to go into hiding. Small groups were seen heading into the hills that overlook Ceuta city, while others concealed themselves in shrubbery and even inside water pipes. Video footage showed Spanish soldiers ordering a 25-year-old migrant to crawl out of a drainage tunnel near the beach.

Many who refused to leave Ceuta appeared to be unaccompanied minors. Some slept outdoors in a disused industrial park. Wandering between abandoned warehouses, the teenagers said they had hardly eaten for four days.

They were among the tens of thousands of migrants who crossed into Ceuta, with most swimming around a border fence that juts out into the Mediterranean. They said they hoped to reach mainland Europe in search of jobs and a better life.

One young man pointed to the badge of the Spanish football shirt he was wearing and said: "Viva España!"

Others shouted "Morocco, no! Spain." One young migrant, who was sleeping on flattened cardboard boxes surrounded by rubbish, said he was 14 years old and had entered Ceuta without his parents or any other adults.

"All the children here want to go to (mainland) Spain," said Aziz Dabch, 41, who was sheltering in the shade of a warehouse.

His 17-year-old daughter said that no one was looking after the unaccompanied minors. "There is no food. We have not eaten today," she said.

In one of the abandoned warehouses, minors milled around aimlessly, while others showered with water from a hosepipe.

Scenes of Spanish police and armed forces chasing migrants back into Morocco have triggered debate about due process, and have also raised questions about applying a similar hardline approach to other borders, including the English Channel.

Spain can legally expel migrants who arrive in Ceuta or Melilla without letting them file an asylum request under controversial laws introduced in 2015. Elsewhere in Europe, this practice is known as "pushbacks" and is only used sporadically.

But the presence of so many minors will complicate the Spanish authorities' attempts to send some of the remaining migrants back across the frontier.

Spanish law dictates that when police identify an undocumented and unaccompanied migrant suspected of being a minor, he or she must be dealt with by child protection services.

The courts then decide whether the child can be returned to his or her country of origin. At the Tarajal border crossing, The Telegraph saw Spanish police transporting migrants, including minors, to the border gate leading back into Morocco.

Immigration lawyers say returning children without following the correct procedures raises legal questions under both Spanish legislation and Spain's obligations under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.

Migrants complained that they were unable to buy anything to eat or drink because many of Ceuta's shops had closed in the wake of the mass incursion.

While many returned to Morocco, escorted by Spanish soldiers and police, others said they were determined to remain.

"They've closed everything down so that we can't buy anything to eat, to force us to return to our country," said Mohamed Hatri, a 23-year-old Moroccan. He said he and others were determined to stay "whether we're hungry or not". There are fears that the situation could grow more volatile as the migrants who have stayed behind demand food and shelter from the authorities.

Some of the remaining migrants were rounded up by the authorities on Sunday.

Outside a housing estate near Ceuta port, Spanish soldiers detained a group of nine tired-looking migrants sitting on the pavement, guarded by troops with an armoured car.

The Spanish have installed a 500-metre (1,640ft) floating boom around Ceuta's seaward frontier as they bolster security measures.

The status of sub-Saharan Africans is likely to be sharply different from that of the Moroccans who entered Ceuta.

The former were fleeing conflict, drought and persecution and may be deemed to have the right to request asylum in the European Union under international law, human rights activists said.

But they will encounter further hardship. Ceuta's migrant reception centre was already overcrowded even before the present crisis erupted. Reports emerged on Sunday of jet skis and motorboats carrying migrants to mainland Spain.

Ceuta, a city of just more than 85,000 inhabitants, was never equipped to deal with a challenge of this magnitude. The local mortuary quickly exceeded capacity, forcing Spain's Military Emergencies Unit to deploy refrigerated trucks from mainland Spain to preserve the bodies recovered from the sea.

Over the weekend, far-Right activists seeking to capitalise on the crisis travelled to Ceuta, saying that the crisis was proof that Europe had lost control of its southern frontier.

They included members of Núcleo Nacional, a Spanish neo-fascist organisation. But the response they encountered was very different from the one they expected.

Hundreds of residents gathered to reject what they said was the political exploitation of a tragedy that has claimed dozens of lives. One of the most striking aspects of the demonstrations was the participation of Ceuta's Muslim community, which represents roughly half of the city's population.

Families, neighbourhood associations and community representatives defended the city's longstanding tradition of coexistence and rejected attempts to use the crisis to promote anti-immigration and anti-Muslim narratives.

Police were deployed to prevent direct clashes between the opposing groups.

Ceuta has long been defined by the coexistence of Christian, Muslim and Jewish communities. That stands in sharp contrast to the increasingly polarised political narrative surrounding the exclave elsewhere in Europe.

The leader of Spain's hard-Right Vox party has called for the border between Ceuta and Morocco to be "militarised" in the wake of what he called an "invasion" of desperate migrants.

Santiago Abascal demanded, "the permanent closure of the border crossing until Rabat provides guarantees that this will never happen again".

He made the remarks during a visit to the Spanish exclave on the North African coast.

"We are facing a brutal attack on our sovereignty, an act of war," said Mr Abascal, calling for "drastic measures" to be taken.

Vox currently commands around 17 per cent of the vote, according to Spanish polls.

authors: Amelia Thomson-Deveaux, Linley Sanders, Mike Catalini, Amelia Thomson-Deveaux, Linley Sanders

Despite that, about 8 in 10 Republicans continue to approve of how Trump is handling immigration.
Republicans are also more likely to approve of how Trump is handling immigration than the economy or Iran.
Immigration remains a strong issue for Trump with Republicans Americans remain divided on whether Trump has overstepped on immigration.
More Republicans approve of how Trump is handling healthcare Healthcare has never been a strong issue for Trump.
text:
WASHINGTON — Immigration remains a stronger issue for President Donald Trump than the economy or Iran, according to a new AP-NORC poll, even after three people were killed in encounters with Immigration and Customs Enforcement in the span of under a week in July.

Trump is not getting a glowing endorsement on his immigration approach from Americans overall, the new survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found. Only 39% of U.S. adults approve of his performance on immigration, a decline from 49% at the beginning of his second term.

Despite that, about 8 in 10 Republicans continue to approve of how Trump is handling immigration. That’s a slight decline from the beginning of Trump’s second term, when about 9 in 10 Republicans approved, but his support on the issue within his base has been mostly stable since last summer despite a chaotic year of immigration enforcement actions.

Republicans are also more likely to approve of how Trump is handling immigration than the economy or Iran. In just the past month, Republican approval of Trump’s handling of Iran dropped slightly in AP-NORC polling

The poll found that about half of U.S. adults say Trump has “gone too far” on deporting immigrants living in the U.S. illegally. That number has also remained steady for over a year, despite multiple immigration crackdowns that deployed federal law enforcement to large cities and at least 10 deaths involving encounters with immigration officers since the mass deportation campaign began. Republicans, however, are much less likely to say Trump has overstepped in his immigration enforcement actions.

Overall, Trump’s popularity has fallen since he took office last year, but the findings highlight the relatively muted impact of the past year’s aggressive immigration enforcement on his public standing. That’s a contrast with views of his handling of Iran, where he’s seen more recent signs of slippage, even among his own supporters.

Immigration remains a strong issue for Trump with Republicans

Americans remain divided on whether Trump has overstepped on immigration.

About half of U.S. adults say Trump has “gone too far” when it comes to restricting legal immigration, in line with the last time the question was asked in February. Roughly half - 47% - say Trump has exceeded his authority when it comes to deporting immigrants living in the U.S. illegally. In each case, about 3 in 10 say Trump’s actions have been “about right,” and closer to 2 in 10 say he hasn’t gone far enough.

Few Republicans – about 2 in 10 or fewer – say he’s “gone too far” on deporting immigrants in the country illegally or restricting legal immigration.

Most Americans, however, say he’s gone too far when it comes to using traffic stops to find and arrest immigrants living in the U.S. illegally - a practice that was at the center of two recent ICE shootings in Maine - and when it comes to sending federal immigration agents into U.S. cities. Republicans were also less likely to see these as oversteps.

James Leatherman, a 68-year-old Republican from San Antonio, is overall supportive of Trump’s handling of the presidency and backs him on immigration in particular.

“You cannot come in here illegally - you’re breaking the law,” he said.

More Americans disapprove than approve of the way ICE is enforcing immigration laws. About half of Americans “strongly” or “somewhat” disapprove of the agency’s approach, while roughly 3 in 10 “strongly” or “somewhat” approve. There’s a wide partisan split, though: About 6 in 10 Republicans approve of ICE’s approach, compared with about 2 in 10 independents and just 4% of Democrats.

Eric Coursen, 76, an independent from Chincoteague, Virginia, agrees with the president that there were issues with the immigration system. He said doesn’t believe in open borders - but he’s deeply opposed to how the administration has been enforcing immigration law.

“It’s like taking some bread when you’re hungry and you take it, you’re going to shoot that person rather than just, you know, get them for theft?” he said. “It’s just overkill.”

Trump’s approval on the economy remains low

About 3 in 10 U.S. adults, 32%, approve of how Trump is handling the economy. That’s down from 40% at the start of his second term, and marks a shift from his first presidential term when the economy was a stronger issue for Trump.

During Trump’s first term, his lowest approval on the economy was 40% in December 2017. Now, his rating is well below that.

Roughly 7 in 10 Republicans – 69% – approve of how Trump is handling the economy. That’s roughly in line with the share who approve of how he’s handing the presidency, but it’s slightly below the 78% who approved early in Trump’s second term.

Leatherman, despite his support for Trump, said he’s feeling the pinch of higher prices in his budget. “I almost have to go to the bank to get a loan before I go grocery shopping,” he said.

About 7 in 10 U.S. adults describe the nation’s economy as “very” or “somewhat” poor, in line with April. Republicans are more optimistic, with about 6 in 10 saying that the U.S. economy is doing well, compared with about 2 in 10 independents and roughly 1 in 10 Democrats.

More Republicans approve of how Trump is handling healthcare

Healthcare has never been a strong issue for Trump. Unlike with immigration and the economy, a clear majority of U.S. adults has disapproved of Trump’s performance on healthcare across both presidential terms. That hasn’t changed in the new poll, which found that only about 3 in 10 Americans approve of how Trump is handling healthcare, in line with when the question was last asked in December.

He’s seen a rebound on the issue among his own supporters since late last year, though. Roughly 71% of Republicans now approve, compared with 59% in the December poll.

That shift comes as Democrats kicked off 100 days until the midterm elections last week, with leaders saying they’ll focus on healthcare cuts, in addition to the cost of living and the war in Iran. Democrats and independents continue to overwhelmingly disapprove of Trump’s handling of healthcare.

___

The AP-NORC poll of 1,165 adults was conducted July 23-27 using a sample drawn from NORC’s probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel, which is designed to be representative of the U.S. population. The margin of sampling error for adults overall is plus or minus 3.7 percentage points. The margin of sampling error is plus or minus 6.0 for Republicans overall and plus or minus 5.4 for Democrats overall.

text:
Representative Thomas Massie accused fellow Republicans of hypocrisy on Saturday, arguing that congressional lawmakers expressing outrage over a massive migrant surge in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta recently supported language in a committee report that appeared sympathetic to Morocco's claims over the territory.

The criticism highlights an unexpected intersection between U.S. legislative politics and an international migration crisis. As Republican leaders in Washington, including President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, pointed to images of tens of thousands of migrants entering Ceuta as a warning about weak borders, Massie contended that his colleagues had previously backed committee report language that appeared sympathetic to Morocco's position on Ceuta and Melilla, the two Spanish enclaves on Morocco's Mediterranean coast.

Newsweek reached out to Massie, the State Department, the House Appropriations Committee Republicans, and the Spanish and Moroccan embassies in Washington, DC for comment on Saturday.

Read More on News

What Massie Said

In a post on X, Massie wrote on Saturday:

"Don't fall for the fake Fox/GOP outrage. Two weeks ago the House passed a bill that greenlighted the transfer of Spanish territory to Morocco. Every Republican except me voted for it, but now THEY are acting shocked at the invasion."

Massie's criticism focused on language contained in the House Appropriations Committee report accompanying the legislation, not on the text of the bill itself.

Massie referenced H.R. 8595, the National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2027. The Kentucky Republican was the sole GOP lawmaker to vote against the legislation, which passed the House on July 15 in a 217-209 vote. Most Democrats opposed the measure.

What the Documents Actually Say

The report Massie cited states: "The Committee notes that the Spanish-administered cities of Ceuta and Melilla are located in Moroccan territory and remain the subject of Morocco's longstanding claim."

It continues: "The Committee supports efforts by the Secretary of State to encourage diplomatic engagement between Morocco and Spain on the future status of Ceuta and Melilla."

The language appears in the report's section on Morocco rather than in the text of H.R. 8595 itself. It is notable because it describes the Spanish-administered cities as being "located in Moroccan territory," wording that aligns with Morocco's longstanding claim to Ceuta and Melilla. However, committee reports are not legally binding and do not themselves alter sovereignty, transfer territory, or change international borders.

That distinction is central to evaluating Massie's claim that Congress "greenlighted the transfer" of Spanish territory to Morocco.

While the report does not endorse transferring sovereignty, it not only describes Ceuta and Melilla as being "located in Moroccan territory" but also expresses support for diplomatic engagement on their "future status," language critics could view as sympathetic to Morocco's position.

Why Ceuta Matters

Ceuta, situated on Morocco's Mediterranean coast, is administered by Spain and forms one of the European Union's few land borders with Africa.

The region plunged into crisis after roughly 50,000 migrants crossed into the enclave on Thursday, prompting the deployment of Spanish military units. Juan Jesús Vivas, head of the Ceuta regional government, described the situation as "absolutely unsustainable."

Spanish authorities later reported that the flow had largely reversed, with more than 48,000 migrants returning to Morocco. Officials confirmed that at least 67 people died during the surge, with some drowning and others crushed while attempting to cross.

U.S. and European Reactions

Trump characterized the scenes as "terrible," while Vance called the footage "an unfortunate reminder of the consequences of mass migration." The State Department stated it stood with Spain against an "egregious violation" of sovereignty.

Other conservative figures echoed those concerns. Senator Eric Schmitt and White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller argued the events illustrated the dangers of permissive immigration policies. In Europe, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni similarly pointed to the surge as a threat to continental security.

Spain and Morocco's Dispute

The political sensitivity of Ceuta extends far beyond migration since Morocco has never accepted Spanish sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla and frequently refers to them as occupied territories.

The issue has repeatedly strained relations between Spain and Morocco.

A previous crisis in 2021 saw roughly 8,000 people enter Ceuta after Morocco relaxed border controls amid tensions with Spain over Western Sahara. Although Spain moved closer to Morocco's position on Western Sahara in 2022, disputes over the enclaves have never completely disappeared.

That history makes the committee report language cited by Massie particularly noteworthy.

The debate highlights how congressional report language, while not legally binding, can carry political significance when lawmakers appear to take conflicting positions on the same international dispute.

title: De-ICE Citizens Bank: A Model of a Successful Civil Resistance Campaign
description:
The De-ICE Citizens Bank campaign had all these ingredients, which is why it succeeded in forcing Citizens Bank to stop financing prison company giants, CoreCivic and GEO Group, operating dozens of detention centers for US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
“No, Citizens Bank won’t credit you at all for its decision, but it is what it is,” MSNBC’s Rachel Maddow said, during a 10-minute segment on the campaign win in late July.
