title: ACLU Files 54 Claims Against Trump Over Deadly ICE Detention Abuse Conditions
description:
The claims have been specifically filed against Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, who are under the president’s executive authority.
Additionally, the rate of deaths in ICE custody has more than doubled due to conditions within the facilities.
The claims have been filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which seeks justice for the victims and their families through financial compensation.
Under the FTCA, “ACLU affiliates are fighting back against the Trump administration’s illegal conduct,” the ACLU said.
Dozens of families and individuals are “seeking justice for the harm they experienced at the hands of federal immigration agents,” and these affiliates are helping them do so.
text:
NEW YORK — Amid allegations of violence, dangerous detention conditions and abuse by federal immigration agents, the American Civil Liberties Union continued its push Wednesday to hold the Trump administration accountable, filing 54 claims in 17 states against the federal government on behalf of people whose rights it says have been repeatedly put in jeopardy.

The claims have been specifically filed against Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, who are under the president’s executive authority. Claims were filed on behalf of people who have “suffered serious violence, abuse, and neglect at the hands of federal law enforcement.”

Since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s term, reports found that ICE agents had “detained more than 10,000 people in five days” in early July 2026 — a noticeable increase from 2024, when ICE officials detained 2,221 individuals from February to August. Additionally, the rate of deaths in ICE custody has more than doubled due to conditions within the facilities.

Human Rights Watch states, “Long-term concerns about US immigration detention include poor conditions in detention facilities, such as unsanitary facilities and inadequate food, which contribute to illness and disease.”

“Food contaminated with worms and mold, limited access to clean drinking water, inadequate medical care” is how Geoffrey Bennett, an American broadcast journalist and co-anchor of PBS NewsHour, described the poor living conditions in ICE detention centers.

Becky Wolozin, a senior lawyer with the National Center for Youth Law, added, “We have seen and heard a lot of things about children not getting child-friendly food, not being able to eat what’s offered. As you mentioned, people reported vegetables that were moldy or had worms in them.”

Additionally, two widely reported death cases for which the ACLU filed claims involved the deaths of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine at the hands of ICE agents. Neither of the victims was the original target of the respective operation.

The claims have been filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which seeks justice for the victims and their families through financial compensation. Under the FTCA, “ACLU affiliates are fighting back against the Trump administration’s illegal conduct,” the ACLU said.

Dozens of families and individuals are “seeking justice for the harm they experienced at the hands of federal immigration agents,” and these affiliates are helping them do so. “Immigrants, U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, families, workers, and people exercising their constitutional rights” have been the victims of this abuse.

One of the individuals being represented is a mother who was being held with her four children and was also five months into a high-risk pregnancy. She and her children were held in a U.S. Customs and Border Protection facility with “limited access to clean running water and without any windows to the outside” for about a month.

Another victim, Norma Bowe, a grandmother, professor, registered nurse and an individual being represented by the ACLU of New Jersey, was “assaulted in front of Delaney Hall by ICE agents while there to operate her mobile health clinic.”

Bowe described the incident: “I was violently attacked by ICE agents while I was trying to provide medical care for people visiting their loved ones in Delaney Hall.”

“ICE agents are acting like they have impunity and are inflicting harm however and whenever they want; without accountability, more people will get hurt and die. ICE must be held responsible,” Bowe said.

“No one should lose their dignity the moment they come face to face with those who hold power,” said Darren, a U.S. citizen who was arrested by Department of Homeland Security agents and “required hospitalization for the chemical irritants they used against him and was left without any of his confiscated property.”

“Federal law enforcement have abused and terrorized countless people,” the ACLU states. “We demand justice for their victims.”

The ACLU will continue to push back against what it describes as the unlawful and inhumane actions of the Trump administration and fight to defend the rights of all.

title: More than 25000 children lose previous legal protections, as federal contract ends
description:
A network of nearly 100 legal groups helps provide children who arrive in ORR custody with legal services, funded by Congress.
But in November, ORR stopped paying for those legal services, after lawyers refused to provide the agency with confidential information it had requested about the children.
ORR refused to renew the contract with the network of legal providers, which expired Friday.
After going more than eight months without pay from ORR, some legal service providers have had to reduce their staff.
On July 29, Acacia received notice from the federal government that ORR was considering a new contract, potentially with different legal providers.
text:
An estimated 26,000 children who entered the U.S. without parents or guardians are expected to be left without independent legal representation as soon as Monday, according to lawyers who help represent them.

For more than two decades, the U.S. has been required by law to protect children who cross the border alone, because of fears that they could be easily exploited, abused or trafficked. After children cross the border unaccompanied, they are typically transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR). A network of nearly 100 legal groups helps provide children who arrive in ORR custody with legal services, funded by Congress.

But in November, ORR stopped paying for those legal services, after lawyers refused to provide the agency with confidential information it had requested about the children. The attorneys say that information is covered by attorney-client privilege.

"The government is withholding payment for work that has already been performed in order to extract confidential information about kids, information the government has no right to," Acacia Center for Justice, the nonprofit that manages the legal services contract with ORR, said in a statement on Thursday.

ORR refused to renew the contract with the network of legal providers, which expired Friday.

Alexa Sendukas, an attorney at the Galveston-Houston Immigrant Representation Project, one of the organizations that provides legal help to migrant children, said that come Monday, the children may have to represent themselves in court and that most who would have to do that would likely end up being deported.

"We know that without a lawyer, unaccompanied children win the right to stay in the United States less than 1% of the time," said Sendukas. "And they've come to the United States seeking safety and protection. And what this administration is asking us to do now is to turn our backs on them completely. And they will undoubtedly be sent to harmful, dangerous situations. And I worry some will be killed if they lose their lawyers."

A group of legal nonprofits filed a lawsuit last year asking a judge to order the government to pay them for what it is owed — some $65 million — and continue paying them for more services. After going more than eight months without pay from ORR, some legal service providers have had to reduce their staff.

"Due to the loss of funding for children's immigration work, ProBAR laid off more than 20% of its staff this week," Lauren Fisher, the legal director of ProBAR, a project of the American Bar Association that provides legal services to children in ORR care, said in an emailed statement on July 31.

On July 29, Acacia received notice from the federal government that ORR was considering a new contract, potentially with different legal providers. But ORR did not share much more information.

"It is not clear who the new contractor will be. They have not answered the questions that we have put to them," said Bettina Rodriguez Schlegel of Acacia, said in response to a question from NPR. "And so there remains a lot of uncertainty and a great deal of concern."

Neither ORR nor the White House responded to NPR's requests for comment about this story.

Almost 1,800 children were in ORR custody in June, according to agency data. ORR has a legal obligation based on a 2008 law to promptly match children with guardians, or "sponsors," in the U.S. who can take care of them. Those children were held in custody for an average of 194 days before being released to sponsors, which lawyers who represent the children say is unusually long and has been detrimental to their health and safety of the children.

For years, lawyers from the network have given presentations for children arriving in ORR care to inform them of their rights and screen them to determine which legal services they are eligible for. Children who are victims of trafficking or abuse, for example, are entitled to special protections. Some of the network's lawyers told NPR they will no longer be able to provide some of those services.

But some of the attorneys say they won't simply abandon the children, even though the contract has not been renewed and they have not been paid by ORR.

"We have an ethical responsibility. We can't just drop a case. If you have a hearing tomorrow, we can't just not show up because the government decided to stop paying us," said Mickey Donovan, the director of legal services at Immigrant Defenders Law Center. "So we'll be there in court on Monday, to introduce ourselves to kids and try to do what we can to prevent their deportation."

title: Colorado inspection law unfairly singles out ICE detention center, operator's lawyers say
authors: Sara Wilson, Lindsey Toomer, Shannon Tyler
description:
Lawyers for the private company that runs Colorado’s only immigration detention center told a judge Friday that a new state law is unfairly discriminatory and should be struck down.
“This (case) isn’t about the general background of public health laws.
The new regulations, he said, present an additional burden outside of existing public health inspection laws.
Yarger argued that the law directly conflicts with the detention center contract GEO has with ICE.
Federal officials are refusing access to local public health inspectors to complete an investigation that’s required by law.
text:
Lawyers for the private company that runs Colorado’s only immigration detention center told a judge Friday that a new state law is unfairly discriminatory and should be struck down.

The GEO Group sued the state over House Bill 26-1276, a new law that requires more frequent health and safety inspections inside immigration detention centers and allows the state to impose civil penalties for noncompliance. GEO operates the facility in Aurora under a contract from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“This (case) isn’t about the general background of public health laws. This isn’t about creating a new inspection authority. This is about a state’s attempt to directly and specifically regulate, through targeted legislation, a single facility in the state,” Fred Yarger, one of GEO’s lawyers, told U.S. District Court Judge Daniel Domenico during a hearing Monday morning.

Yarger said that because there is only one facility in the state subject to the “bespoke” new law, it is discriminatory. The new regulations, he said, present an additional burden outside of existing public health inspection laws.

“It’s not simply the same (inspection) regime as before. If it was, the General Assembly would not have passed (the law),” he said.

GEO Group sues over new Colorado law requiring immigration detention center safety inspections

The state cannot regulate the federal government, Yarger said, but it is circumventing that restriction by regulating the government’s contractor instead. The law specifically carves out facilities directly operated by the federal government and it instead applies to contractor-operated facilities that “house or detain individuals who are noncitizens for purposes of civil immigration proceedings.”

That can only apply to the GEO site in Aurora.

GEO is asking the court to issue a preliminary injunction against the new law, which Democrats in the Legislature passed this year. It sets a minimum number of yearly health and safety inspections at the facility, requires GEO to pay for those inspections and lets the attorney general bring civil penalties against the company for noncompliance. Its provisions also cover how minors can be detained, mental health worker staffing minimums and annual reporting requirements.

Yarger argued that the law directly conflicts with the detention center contract GEO has with ICE. That contract requires that medical workers, including mental health professionals, are available at all times, but the new law states that someone must be physically on site. The contract also requires that GEO abide by ICE’s determination about access. Domenico questioned why he shouldn’t assume those contractual provisions with ICE include the expectation that GEO will comply with state and local laws.

Yarger said “the notion that through this contract, the (U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security) consented to any state law … it’s not a fair reading of the contract.”

Concerns are speculative

Talia Kraemer, representing the state, contended that there are no current or imminent threats to GEO, because the parts of the law that impose new requirements, such as around medical workers, have not undergone the rulemaking process through the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment. That could take many months and would include an opportunity for input from GEO. The company’s concerns are speculative, she said.

Kraemer said the state only views the section related to inspections as in effect. In fact, state lawyers said, GEO has had favorable treatment historically because it has faced fewer required inspections than other penal facilities like state prisons and county jails.

“The fact the General Assembly has imposed a minimum inspections … does not indicate that Aurora has been singled out,” state lawyer Gabriel Podesta said.

Domenico asked the state’s lawyers where the constitutional line is when it comes to regulations of federal contractors.

“What if the regulations the state wanted to impose were so onerous that, maybe it didn’t make it impossible, but … that would make it effectively that nobody could profitably operate one of these?” he said. “Does it make sense to say ‘Well, the federal government contracts, and they’re allowed to comply with their contractural provisions, and anything beyond that is interfering with the federal government’s chosen methods?”

Domenico said he will issue a written order on the matter “as soon as possible.”

Tuberculosis case

The litigation coincides with GEO and ICE refusing to comply with a public health order issued by the Adams County Health Department around a confirmed tuberculosis case at the detention center. Federal officials are refusing access to local public health inspectors to complete an investigation that’s required by law.

“Adams County’s legal counsel, alongside the Colorado Attorney General’s Office, is actively working to preserve public health authority and ensure ACHD can continue fulfilling its statutory responsibilities in litigation arising from challenges brought by The GEO Group,” ACHD Executive Director Kelly Weidenbach said in a statement. “While that legal process moves forward, ACHD’s responsibility remains unchanged. We will continue to follow the science, apply Colorado’s public health laws consistently, and work with our partners to protect the health of every person and every community we serve.”

Vietnamese national Phu Nguyen was intercepted by two immigration agents in plain clothes on July 13 at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, Nevada, CNN reported.
However, Nguyen, whose visa expired in 2015, was arrested the next day when he arrived at Los Angeles International Airport in California.
Entering an airport is like walking into their web: ICE has a presence at every airport,” immigration lawyer Alex Gálvez explained.
The lawyer has been warning migrants since last year about the risks of going to an airport.
text:
The option that for years allowed undocumented migrants to travel on domestic flights has come to an end under the Donald Trump administration. A new directive from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) orders its agents to stop them at airports, eliminating one of the few ways to travel without the risk of crossing an international border. For years, those flights were a relatively safe alternative to visit family, work, study, or simply see other parts of the country. That reality has now changed. The move adds to the large-scale deportation campaign driven by the White House and to a strategy aimed at increasing pressure on migrants until they return to their home communities voluntarily.

In a statement, DHS confirmed it has revoked a policy “that allowed foreigners who are in our country illegally to travel by air within the national territory.” The agency called that practice “harmful” and attributed it to the administration of former president Joe Biden (2021–2025), although it was also tolerated under past Republican administrations. “This administration works diligently to ensure that foreigners who are in our country illegally can no longer fly, unless it is to leave the country and self-deport,” the statement sent to EL PAÍS warns.

However, the agency has not disclosed when the new directive took effect, how many people have been detained, or at which airports it is being enforced. This newspaper asked the administrators and police forces at some of the country’s largest airports, including those in Los Angeles, New York, and Chicago, about these operations. All declined to comment.

The New York Times, the first outlet to report on the practice, said more than 25 people from over a dozen countries were recently detained at U.S. airports, from California to Virginia, as part of the new measure. The report, based on DHS documents and interviews with lawyers representing some of those arrested, says immigration agents in plain clothes have intercepted migrants while they were completing pre-flight documentation checks or waiting in boarding areas in at least 15 airports.

“ICE is here!”

One such case is that of Ecuadorian Chantal Alejandra Morales Rojas, 27, who was detained on July 20 by federal agents in plain clothes moments before boarding a Southwest Airlines flight at Denver International Airport in Colorado. The South American was returning home to Oakland, California. “ICE is here! Help us!” a woman was heard shouting as she begged other passengers for help. No one intervened.

Morales Rojas was taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Her lawyer told The New York Times that she had entered the country legally on a visa and had filed an application to remain in the United States. DHS, however, said the woman “overstayed her visa” and for that reason was subject to deportation proceedings. On July 30, she was released after posting bond.

Among those now being targeted by ICE are thousands of people like Morales Rojas, whose status falls into a zone of legal uncertainty: foreigners waiting for an extension of their immigration status, approval of permanent residency, or other paperwork that would allow them to remain in the country. They were not previously priorities for detention, but they are now on the blacklist as the Trump administration seeks to meet a goal of 2,000 immigration arrests per day.

Vietnamese national Phu Nguyen was intercepted by two immigration agents in plain clothes on July 13 at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, Nevada, CNN reported. A video of the incident shows him lying on the ground while one officer pins him down and swats at the person recording the scene with a cellphone. Authorities say the agents chose to withdraw to avoid escalating tensions among passengers. However, Nguyen, whose visa expired in 2015, was arrested the next day when he arrived at Los Angeles International Airport in California.

Days later, a Ukrainian woman was arrested under similar circumstances at San Francisco International Airport, also for being in the country on a visa that had expired in 2011. At least 11 migrants living in that area of California have been detained at U.S. airport terminals in recent days, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.

Easier arrests

“Immigration authorities are seeking tactics that require fewer resources to carry out arrests. Entering an airport is like walking into their web: ICE has a presence at every airport,” immigration lawyer Alex Gálvez explained. The attorney compares these operations to the “controlled” arrests the agency has carried out in courthouses, immigration offices, and other places where federal authorities know it is easier to locate and arrest undocumented migrants. They know precisely what time the person they want to detain will arrive, unlike an operation at someone’s home, where uncertainty is greater and the deployment requires more time, personnel, and resources.

These operations at airline terminals are attributed to an expanded collaboration between ICE and the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), the agency created after the September 11, 2001 attacks to strengthen airport security. That cooperation became visible in March, when dozens of ICE agents (identifiable by their vests with insignia and, in many cases, without the hoods they often use to cover their faces during immigration raids) were deployed to more than a dozen airports across the country. Their presence responded to TSA staffing shortages caused by a partial federal government shutdown after budget negotiations in Congress stalled.

Another example of the close cooperation between the two agencies is the more than 800 detainees who ended up in ICE custody thanks to information provided by the TSA, according to a Reuters report.

“People don’t realize that when they buy an airplane ticket it’s as if they text ICE their name, date of birth, and practically ask them to track their information to confirm their immigration status,” Gálvez says. The lawyer has been warning migrants since last year about the risks of going to an airport. In a video that went viral when ICE agents were deployed to terminals to support the TSA, Gálvez issued this warning, which now feels even more relevant: “If you’re undocumented and plan to travel by plane, it’s very dangerous. It’s almost like putting your head in the wolf’s mouth.”

“Martinez-Ballinas repeatedly and flagrantly disregarded the laws of the United States and faces deportation for the third time,” said ERO Newark Acting Field Office Director Arthur J. Wilson, Jr. “His conviction for an automotive offense that resulted in the tragic loss of a U.S. Marine in 2017 demonstrates a complete lack of respect for human life and our legal system. In 2021, U.S. Border Patrol arrested Martinez-Ballinas trying to cross the southern border in the Rio Grande Valley, Texas. He was convicted of illegal reentry in the Southern District of Texas and sentenced to 15 months in prison. Undeterred, ICE removed Martinez-Ballinas a second time in October 2022. Due to the Biden administration’s open border debacle, Martinez -Ballinas was able to illegally enter the United States again completely undetected. ICE ultimately apprehended Martinez -Ballinas in Maryland in December 2023.

Martinez remains in ICE custody in New Jersey pending his third removal from the United States.

text:
The Trump administration plans to spend $1.6 billion through September 2027 in its partnerships with state and local police participating in immigration enforcement, a sum that far exceeds previous funding.

The massive money boost to the Department of Homeland Security through the 2025 reconciliation law fully funds the 287(g) program, according to the department.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement outlined its strategy for spending $100 million in the last fiscal year, $575 million this fiscal year and $475 million in fiscal 2027 for detention and removal operations under these agreements, according to a document publicly released earlier this month.

DHS’s Office of the Secretary and Executive Management also has spent $460 million for 287(g) ICE personnel assignments this fiscal year, according to Office of Management and Budget records.

Trending

The 287(g) program is part of a federal law that allows ICE to delegate some federal immigration enforcement powers to state and local law enforcement.

The fastest growing subset of agreements with local police, known as the Task Force Model, deputizes law enforcement to detain and arrest people they suspect live in the country without authorization.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin recently called the 287(g) program “the greatest partnership we can have.”

“We say to the local law enforcement and the state law enforcement … ‘If you run across these individuals, keep them,’” Mullin said during a press conference in June. “‘We will pay for your time and some of the equipment, just hold them and we will come pick them up.’”

The number of monthly 287(g) arrests spiked from 301 in January 2025 to 3,388 in January 2026 but dropped down to 2,630 in February, according to the Deportation Data Project.

New sign-ups under the program have soared, according to ICE’s database. Of the 2,179 partnerships across the country, 67% allow for street-level immigration enforcement. The Trump administration has advertised $7,500 for equipment per trained officer, $100,000 for new vehicles per partnership, salary and benefits reimbursement and overtime funds.

Since January 2025, the agreements have increased by more than 1470%, according to an analysis from FWD.us, a policy organization that opposes the partnerships between local police and ICE.

“It’s really important to be thinking about the effects on immigrants, but also the effects on local communities and citizens in the U.S. to all of this new money pouring in with very little oversight,” said Felicity Rose, the group’s vice president of criminal justice research and policy.

Even though the first Trump administration also saw an increase in 287(g) agreements from 35 to 150, the funding remained stagnant at $24.3 million annually, despite ICE’s efforts to request more funding, according to end-of-year reports the agency submitted to Congress.

“Without the funding increase, the program expansion will be challenged,” Matthew Albence, ICE’s then-acting director, wrote in a fiscal year 2019 report on the program. At the time, ICE unsuccessfully sought $77 million for fiscal 2021.

Before the 2025 cash infusion, the most money ICE had gotten for 287(g) had been $68 million under President Barack Obama, according to the yearly reports. The annual funding also dropped to $24.3 million during the Obama administration, which discontinued its use of the Task Force Model after findings of civil-rights abuses, including racial targeting by the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office in Arizona.

The $1.6 billion is not the only funding ICE could use for the revival of the local partnerships. Billions more from this year’s reconciliation bill can be used for the 287(g) program through 2029. ICE’s spend plan only covers the program through fiscal year 2027, and the agency didn’t respond to questions as to whether it would maintain the same level of funding after that.

text:
The operator of Colorado’s only immigrant detention center is still refusing to allow state health inspectors to conduct an investigation into a tuberculosis case in the facility, a month after officials issued an order requiring access.

Amid the standoff, the company—Geo Group, which operates the facility for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement—argued in federal court Friday that a new state law requiring more regular inspections at the facility should be struck down as unconstitutional.

For the past month, Geo Group has ignored a public health order from Adams County officials seeking access to the Aurora detention center so that they can conduct an investigation into the TB case, which was confirmed late last month. Company officials have also not responded to efforts by the county to communicate about the situation. The company hasn’t complied with a request by Colorado’s top public health official that sought inspector access by July 17.

State and local officials have not yet taken additional steps, such as seeking a court order, to obtain access to the facility.

Kelly Weidenbach, the executive director of the Adams County Health Department, told reporters outside federal court Friday in Denver that the county was still assessing options with its legal counsel and state officials.

Asked why the department hadn’t gone to court to enforce its order, Weidenbach said Geo’s ongoing legal effort to invalidate House Bill 1276 — which requires multiple health inspections of the facility each year — have played a role in officials’ planning.

“Some of the legal arguments in this particular case were pertinent to our authority,” she said.

Hope Schuler, a spokeswoman for the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, said in a Thursday email that the state was also still evaluating “whether additional state action, including a state public health order, would meaningfully improve access or simply duplicate requirements already in place.” If the state issued its own health order that Geo ignored, then the Colorado Attorney General’s Office could seek a court order to enforce it.

Schuler said the state health department had been told that the patient who tested positive for TB had been isolated and then left the facility; federal officials said the person was deported. Schuler said the facility undertook testing and contact tracing, which is the process of tracking down who may have been in contact with the infected patient.

“That information, if true, is reassuring, but it remains summary-level, though we are not able to independently verify the information,” Schuler wrote. “Public health officials are continuing to ask to verify that everyone potentially exposed was appropriately identified, tested, and treated.”

Weidenbach said the patient who tested positive for TB last month appears to have contracted the condition outside of the facility and that the patient denied having symptoms. She said health officials didn’t have any information on whether other patients had contracted TB.

According to information published by U.S. Rep. Jason Crow’s office, Geo officials said earlier this month that there was one detainee who was still being monitored for TB. The facility’s staff told Crow’s office that they held a “medical town hall for detainees in the affected area” and that some asked to be tested.

From Geo’s investigation, the facility determined that 61 individuals were exposed to the sick patient and were placed in a “precautionary cohort.” Crow’s office said at least two detainees were in medical isolation.

“When asked, ICE said they can deny facility access to local officials as they are a federal facility. GEO medical staff said they adhere to CDC guidelines,” Crow’s office wrote, referencing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Geo officials have taken that argument into federal court.

On Friday, attorneys for the company told U.S. District Court Judge Daniel D. Domenico that the state cannot discriminate against Geo by subjecting it to “bespoke” inspection protocols. They also said that other provisions in the bill — like specific medical staffing levels and new processes related to communicable diseases — could not be levied against the company because it’s a federal contractor.

But attorneys for the state countered that the detention center, if anything, had received favorable treatment because it had previously faced a lower health inspection burden than state prisons and county jails. They pointed out that Geo has been subject to inspections by state officials for several years and had not challenged that authority before.

As for the other provisions in the new law, the attorneys said those were subject to rulemaking by the state health department and were not going to be implemented in the imminent future.

Geo asked Domenico to immediately block the law. The judge said he would issue a ruling on whether to do so at a later date.

title: End of temporary status for Haitians in US sets off scramble for options - CSMonitor.com
authors: Cameron Pugh, The Christian Science Monitor
description:
Amda moved to Massachusetts with her family in August 2023, entering the country through a Biden-era humanitarian program.
Why We Wrote This The loss of temporary status for some 334,000 Haitian and Syrian immigrants has families weighing other options, which generally don’t include returning to their troubled countries.
Those who have lived and worked in the U.S. under the program now face revoked work authorization and possible deportation.
“Temporary Protected Status is exactly that – temporary,” a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson wrote in a statement.
More than 10,000 Haitians with TPS work in Massachusetts, according to FWD.us, a criminal justice and immigration policy organization.
text:
By now, Amda is closely acquainted with instability. It’s the word that’s often used to describe her native Haiti, which has been all but torn apart by gangs and natural disasters. Although her new home of Massachusetts has brought relief from those challenges, “instability” still describes her time in the United States.

Amda moved to Massachusetts with her family in August 2023, entering the country through a Biden-era humanitarian program. In 2025, the Trump administration canceled that program, and she applied for temporary protected status (TPS), which similarly provided defense against deportation, a work permit, and some peace of mind.

“When we did the application for TPS, we thought it would give us some time to figure out what we should do,” Amda says. She requested that her full name be withheld for fear of being targeted by immigration officials.

Why We Wrote This

The loss of temporary status for some 334,000 Haitian and Syrian immigrants has families weighing other options, which generally don’t include returning to their troubled countries. Massachusetts’ large Haitian community has the support of those who recognize the potential impact of its absence.

But now, she, her family, and hundreds of thousands more, face instability once again.

TPS was officially slated to end this week for some 334,000 Haitians and Syrians, after the Supreme Court in June upheld the government’s bid to rescind protections. Those who have lived and worked in the U.S. under the program now face revoked work authorization and possible deportation. The Trump administration has long seen TPS, which the government grants to foreigners for whom returning home is unsafe, as a back door to remain in the country long-term.

“Temporary Protected Status is exactly that – temporary,” a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson wrote in a statement. “For too long, TPS has been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program despite Congress never intending it to be permanent.”

Some confusion remains about whether the program has truly ended yet, as lawyers and the government trade different interpretations of the Supreme Court’s decision. Regardless, few places will feel the ripples of the decision more than Massachusetts, where some 66,600 Haitian immigrants, including 22,600 TPS holders, live. Immigrant advocates here describe the country’s third-largest Haitian population rushing to make plans for an unknown future: giving up guardianship of their American-born children, contemplating international moves, and, in many cases, simply hoping that Immigration and Customs Enforcement doesn’t knock on their doors.

“It is no longer simply an immigration policy issue,” says Pastor Dieufort Fleurissaint, who runs the True Alliance Center in Boston, a faith-based immigrant advocacy organization. “It is becoming a workforce, family stability, healthcare, [and] housing [issue].”

Country in crisis

For Amda, one thing is clear: Returning to Haiti is not an option.

It’s not that she doesn’t want to. In Port-au-Prince, Haiti’s capital, she worked as a pharmacist and doctor. She dreams of one day returning as an anesthesiologist and helping her homeland recover.

But life in Haiti became untenable when her family became a target for gangs. The assassination of its last elected president, in 2021, plunged Haiti into a violent crisis. Gangs have seized up to 90% of Port-au-Prince, according to the United Nations, displacing some 1.5 million people nationally. The economy is in tatters, and food insecurity is widespread. The U.S. State Department recommends against traveling there for “any reason” because of “the risk of crime, terrorism, kidnapping, unrest, and limited health care.”

“There’s no way for us to live there. Most of our family had to leave the country as well,” she says. Living in Haiti, “you’re in survival mode. It’s not really a life.”

Haiti first received TPS designation in 2010, after a 7 magnitude earthquake devastated the island nation. The designation, originally for 18 months, had been repeatedly extended since. Although TPS provides no separate pathway to citizenship or permanent residency, many of its beneficiaries have lived in the U.S. for decades.

To supporters of President Donald Trump, that’s created an unsustainable program with no clear end goal. There comes a point, they argue, when the U.S. cannot be expected to be responsible for disasters elsewhere.

“The Trump administration is taking the program and putting it back in the box of what it was supposed to be in the first place,” says Simon Hankinson, who studies immigration policy at The Heritage Foundation and served in the foreign service for over two decades. “Successive administrations have kicked the can down the road, and this never should have been allowed to get out of control.”

In canceling the benefit last year, the government said that the “situation in Haiti remains concerning” but that the U.S. “must prioritize its national interests.” Immigration officials plan to ramp up enforcement actions against Haitians, according to news reports. In a statement to the Monitor, DHS declined to comment on “ongoing or future operations.”

Amda and her family applied for asylum last year, anticipating that they might need another defense against deportation after their initial permission expired. For now, they’ve been shielded from deportation and have been able to work while their application moves through the system. Although the two programs similarly target humanitarian concerns, being a TPS holder does not guarantee asylum, which requires that applicants prove they’ve been persecuted on specific grounds.

Uncertain future

In mid-July, over 100 people gathered under trees outside Boston City Hall. Local advocacy groups and politicians had organized a campaign pushing not only a humanitarian argument for keeping TPS, but also an economic one.

More than 10,000 Haitians with TPS work in Massachusetts, according to FWD.us, a criminal justice and immigration policy organization. Immigrants make up 47% of workers tending to people in long-term care facilities here, a 2026 report from KFF said.

“It’s a complete disregard for human beings who have not only worked here, but also contributed so much to the economy,” says Geralde Gabeau, founder of the Immigrant Family Services Institute in Boston and a native of Haiti.

Amda, like one-fifth of Haitians living in the U.S., works in healthcare. Nationwide, 88% of TPS holders are in the labor force, according to the Latino Policy & Politics Initiative at the University of California, Los Angeles.

“We don’t have that security,” says Amda, who works as a medical assistant. “Even if you’re working at a hospital doing 12-hour shifts, helping people you don’t even know.”

Mr. Hankinson dismisses the economic arguments, saying that there will be plenty of demand from American citizens and immigrants who retain legal status for any jobs left vacant by TPS holders.

As of late July, Amda and her family still have work permits – and each other. When she first arrived in Massachusetts, she worried she would never get used to the bitter cold. Even the August heat was nothing compared with Haiti.

Now, her “heart is in Massachusetts,” and life goes on. She’s eyeing going back to school to train as a physician assistant, and she still wants to become an anesthesiologist. Her mother continues working. Her father is working on his English after recently starting classes. And her sister, Amda says, just got married.

text:
The White House is using Bad Bunny and Drake songs to soundtrack videos promoting President Donald Trump’s deportation campaign, sparking backlash from fans and raising questions about the use of the artists’ music.

A video posted Thursday (July 30) to the White House’s TikTok account features Bad Bunny’s “La Mudanza” — which reached No. 51 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 2025 — over quick-cut images of Trump, followed by footage of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers detaining undocumented men and women. The video displays the lyric “un aplauso para mami y papi porque en verdad rompieron” — “a round of applause for mom and dad, because they really crushed it” — alongside altered text in the clip that reads, “A round of applause for Donald J. Trump because he really crushed it.”

The post’s caption reads, “We’re making America great again.”

The video, which the president’s supporters praised, also immediately drew outrage in the comments, with users writing, “I know you f–king didn’t!!!!,” “The audacity!” and “Do not disrespect Bad Bunny like that.” Others criticized the administration’s immigration policies, writing, “No one is illegal on stolen land.”

The White House followed the Bad Bunny post with another music-driven deportation video on Friday (July 31), this time using Drake’s “Hoe Phase,” the opening track from his MADE OF HONOUR album, which reached No. 3 on the Billboard 200. That clip features helicopters, airplanes, footage of the U.S.-Mexico border and scenes of people being detained by ICE. Its caption reads, “Let us remind you if you’re here illegally, you’re going home,” while text in the video says, “Did you forget about back home?” — a lyric from Drizzy’s song.

Like the previous video featuring Bad Bunny’s track, the TikTok featuring Drake’s tune saw commenters critize the president, with several wondering “Did you forget about those files?” in reference to the Epstein files. (The president has previously denied any wrongdoing as it relates to Epstein.)

Billboard has reached out to representatives for Bad Bunny and Drake, as well as the White House, for comment.

The videos arrive as Trump continues to make the removal of undocumented people a priority of his administration. Since returning to the White House in January 2025, the twice-impeached president has expanded immigration enforcement and pushed for a sweeping mass-deportation effort, with ICE arrests and removals becoming a defining part of his domestic agenda.

Bad Bunny — who is from Puerto Rico, a territory of the U.S. — has been an outspoken critic of ICE operations and the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. At the 2026 Grammy Awards, the Puerto Rican superstar said during his acceptance speech for best música urbana album, “We’re not savage, we’re not animals, we’re not aliens. We are humans, and we are Americans.”

Drake, who is from Toronto, has also spoken out against the president in the past. During the rapper’s February 2017 show in London on his Boy Meets World Tour, he shared his thoughts on the business mogul, who had just taken office for his first term. “Every day I wake up and see all this bulls–t going in the world, people trying to tear us apart, people trying to make us turn against each other,” he said at the time. “My proudest moment — take a look around at this room, you’ll people from all races and all places.”

He added: “If you think one man can tear this world apart, you’re out of your motherf–king mind. It’s on us to keep this s–t together. F–k that man.”

text:
by Leilah Ortega, Nevada Current

Nevada Democratic U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto this week called President Trump’s immigration policies “extreme” and “un-American” and said former President Biden “placed too little emphasis on border security.”

“I think I speak for everyone here when I say that we thoroughly understand the failures of the Trump administration’s immigration agenda,” Cortez Masto said during a speech at a Center for American Progress event in Washington, D.C. Wednesday.

“Every day, we’re hearing about masked agents without identification coming into our neighborhoods with the intention of intimidating and attacking immigrants. ICE agents are attacking peaceful protestors and killing American citizens.”

While Cortez Masto criticized the Trump administration, she said “the Biden administration did not handle immigration policy well either.”

The Biden administration placed “too much emphasis on supporting the newly arriving asylum seekers,” she said, and overlooked undocumented immigrants who lived in the United States for decades.

Cortez Masto this week reintroduced the Fairness for Immigrant Families Act, which failed to pass in 2021. The bill would eliminate three- and 1o- year immigration bars, which block undocumented immigrants from reentering the United States after they leave or get deported for three or 10 years after residing in the country without legal status.

Cortez Masto said the bill would reestablish the 245 (i) program, which allows undocumented immigrants to adjust their legal status by paying a penalty fee and is only eligible for those who filed for the program on or before April 30, 2001. The bill also promises to protect DACA recipients, parents of U.S. citizen children, and immigrants with pending applications from deportation, and crack down on fraudulent immigration services.

“The legislation pulls down some of the arbitrary barriers in our current immigration laws that keep people undocumented with no way of fixing their status,” she said. “It protects immigrant families from fraud. And it’s been updated to address the new threats we’re seeing under the second Trump administration.”

Cortez Masto described her proposal as a way for the nation to learn from past mistakes and “offer pragmatic solutions to our country’s broken immigration system.”

But, with a Republican majority in the Senate and Trump still in office, the bill is not likely to pass.

Cortez Masto did not directly condemn ICE in her comments, but she acknowledged the community fear surrounding the organization, stating detainment based on physical appearance “erodes all Americans’ civil liberties.”

Cortez Masto also commented on the current administration’s intentional delay of DACA renewals and the fear immigrant families face daily, calling it “horrific” and “unacceptable.”

Along with the emotional factors, she highlighted the positive economic impact of immigrants. Undocumented immigrants contributed over $37 billion in state and local taxes in 2022, according to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy. In Nevada, undocumented immigrants accounted for over $500 million of that amount.

title: Immigrant children could face court hearings without lawyers, Chicago attorneys warn
authors: Rose Schmidt, Lisa Capitanini, Richard Moy
description:
New concerns have emerged from immigration attorneys that about 26,000 vulnerable immigrant children across the nation could face deportations -- without lawyers to represent them in court.
That includes the Chicago-based Children's Legal Center, which represents children in Illinois and Indiana.
Recently, at least two unaccompanied children in the Chicago area were ordered removed from the country, according to Smith.
"The child that was ordered removed just two weeks ago (was fully) crying after the immigration court hearing.
And it's horrible that we are doing this to children," Smith said.
text:
New concerns have emerged from immigration attorneys that about 26,000 vulnerable immigrant children across the nation could face deportations -- without lawyers to represent them in court.

On Friday, two Illinois members of Congress, U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin and Rep. Bill Foster, toured a shelter that houses about 20 unaccompanied children who fled bad situations in their home countries.

Durbin said his visit with unaccompanied minors is one he'll remember for a long time.

"These kids have been abused. They have been neglected. They've been abandoned. They've been trafficked. And this agency is trying to give them a life," Durbin said.

The children's attorney, Laura Smith, said recent Department of Justice policy changes leave the children at risk of deportation, even though she believes they qualify for a protection created by Congress called Special Immigrant Juvenile Status, which would give them a pathway to citizenship.

"The children walk into court thinking, 'ICE is going to take me right now,' and they walk in with fear, and they're doing that every 14 to 21 days now because of the policy changes of this administration," said Smith, who is the executive director of the Children’s Legal Center.

Smith believes the risks of the children being removed from the United States are even greater after Friday because that was when the federal contract providing children across the country with legal representation expired.

"The practical implication is children will then go to court without an attorney, 5-year-olds, 6-year-olds, 10-year-olds," Smith said. "They don't understand the immigration process. Many of the general public don't understand the immigration process because it is extremely complicated, and it's even more complicated for unaccompanied minors."

The contract is between the federal Office of Refugee Resettlement and the Acacia Center for Justice, which has immigration attorneys subcontracting around the country.

That includes the Chicago-based Children's Legal Center, which represents children in Illinois and Indiana. The center said it hasn't received payments from the federal government since December. Smith and other immigration attorneys allege the Trump administration is withholding payments until they turn over what they describe as sensitive information about these children.

In a statement, the Office of Refugee Resettlement, or ORR, told us it "remains fully compliant with legal and regulatory obligations and does not act in any way that could dissuade a child from seeking appropriate legal relief."

ORR said it offered Acacia the opportunity to extend the contract if Acacia provides data about its clients and bills ORR when it submits applications for immigration relief.

Recently, at least two unaccompanied children in the Chicago area were ordered removed from the country, according to Smith. Those orders are being appealed.

"The child that was ordered removed just two weeks ago (was fully) crying after the immigration court hearing. Complete devastation. And it's horrible that we are doing this to children," Smith said.

NBC 5 also reached out to the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice for comment but hadn't heard back as of Friday evening.

title: Michael Smolens: It's a no-brainer — DACA is good for San Diego, America vice today.

He said DACA recipients contribute about $968 million annually to the regional economy.

text:
San Diego leaders across the spectrum lay out economic and social benefits of program providing temporary legal status for young immigrant "Dreamers"

A broad spectrum of San Diego business, labor, community and political leaders sent a straightforward message this week.

The Trump administration must stop suspiciously long delays in approving renewal applications for Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients that are threatening their ability to work and remain in the country.

But they had a broader, equally important goal: to remind the public that people with DACA status are a boon to the economy in San Diego and the country at large. Not only should renewals be expedited, they said, but recipients should be given permanent residency status.

At a Tuesday news conference outside the downtown office of the U.S. Customs and Immigration Service (USCIS), Rep. Scott Peters, D-San Diego, noted that to qualify for DACA, immigrants must show they are working or in school or in the military — and, he added, “most important, you can’t be in trouble with the law.

“By definition, people covered by the DACA program are the kind of people we want to join us as Americans,” he said.

In 2025, the median wait time for renewals was 15 days. In February of this year, it was 70 days, according to USCIS data, an increase of more than 400 percent. About 8,000 immigrant “Dreamers,” as DACA recipients are often called, reside in the San Diego region and some 500,000 across the country.

“For more than a decade, Dreamers have strengthened our economy,” said Chris Cate, president and CEO of the San Diego Regional Chamber of Commerce and a former Republican City Council member.

He said DACA recipients contribute about $968 million annually to the regional economy.

The DACA boost to the economy is not a new story. But given that Trump is ramping up efforts to undermine the program — courts so far have blocked him from ending it outright — it’s a story that needs to be revisited regularly.

In terms of raw dollars and cents, the country would lose a great deal if DACA no longer existed, in addition to negative cultural and societal impacts.

More than 80 percent of DACA recipients are in the workforce, according to FWD.us, an organization focused on immigration and criminal justice reform.

Years ago, the Democratic Joint Economic Committee in Congress estimated DACA recipients could add $460 billion to the U.S. economy over the next decade. That was based on 2017 data, when there were about 800,000 DACA recipients.

“DACA recipients contributed, on net, roughly $3.4 billion annually to the federal balance sheet” in 2018, according to the American Action Forum.

DACA was created by President Barack Obama in 2012 to give temporary protection from deportation and grant work permits to qualified undocumented immigrants who were brought to the country as children. Recipients must reapply every two years to keep their status.

The average DACA recipient is 33 years old and has lived in the U.S. for 27 years, according to FWD.us. It’s the only country most have ever really known.

Almost all have graduated from high school, and nearly half have some college education. About a third are married, and a little more than that have at least one child at home.

Public support for Dreamers has been strong for years. A Gallup poll released this month found 81 percent of Americans support allowing immigrants who were brought to the U.S. illegally as children the chance to become U.S. citizens if they meet certain requirements over a period of time.

Democrats and independents overwhelmingly were in favor, as were 56 percent of Republicans.

Courts have kept DACA alive amid challenges by the Trump administration and Republican-run states. While judges allowed renewals for existing participants, they blocked any new applications.

The program has been under assault by Trump since 2017, his first year in the White House, when he tried to kill the program. The fate of DACA is still in the hands of the courts.

Trump has said a lot of nasty things about undocumented immigrants over the years, but his tone has been different about DACA recipients, for whom he has expressed empathy while trying to take away their temporary status.

“We love the Dreamers,” he has said. Just before the start of his current term, he said “we have to do something” to help them.

But the president, who at times has shown disregard for the Constitution, contends that the Obama-created program is unconstitutional and must be approved by Congress.

At one point, Trump probably could have ordered his compliant Republican congressional majorities to achieve a DACA remedy along with like-minded Democrats, but he hasn’t in recent years. Long-ago efforts to give DACA recipients certainty had bogged down in partisan jockeying between Republicans and Democrats.

Prospects of him doing so now seem even more remote, given his dreadful polling numbers — including slippage among Republicans — and potential for alienating his core MAGA base.

DACA critics also have said the program acts as an incentive for illegal immigration, rewards law-breaking, and is unfair to immigrants seeking to come here legally.

Meanwhile, the USCIS has added requirements and expanded security checks for DACA renewals that have slowed the process. Recipients are being advised to reapply much earlier than before.

It’s a familiar Trump administration tactic to deny people government benefits. People are falling out of Medicaid and food stamp programs after the administration enacted more onerous qualifying requirements.

Frustration among the San Diego leaders over DACA delays was palpable on Tuesday.

“They’ve already been approved and vetted,” said Trevor Moore, vice president of the commercial real estate firm Cush Enterprises, whose company counts many small businesses among its clients, including restaurants.

Arcela Nuñez-Alvarez, co-founder and co-director of Universidad Popular, a community-based civic organization, said renewals of 54,000 DACA recipients nationwide are being held up.

“The American Dream has turned into a nightmare overnight,” she said.

The community leaders largely stayed away from Trump’s broader immigration crackdown, which is also impacting the workforce, though no doubt some have strong opinions about it.

They were trying to keep DACA in the public eye as immigration headlines are often dominated by Trump’s mass deportations and aggressive federal immigration raids that have resulted in agents shooting and killing protesters and targets of enforcement.

Carol Kim, executive secretary-treasurer of the San Diego and Imperial Counties Labor Council, said the Trump squeeze on DACA and immigration in general is impacting numerous sectors, including construction and healthcare research. That, in turn, she said, can impact such things as infrastructure projects and medical advancements.

“We all pay the price,” she said.

title: Immigrants at FDC Miami: 'Animals get treated better than this' | WLRN
description:
“Animals get treated better than this,” Cervelo Trujillo told Castellanos over the phone.
Dumont told his wife that he served food at FDC, and saw cockroaches in the supply earlier this month.
“I saw the cockroach on the cart where the food comes in,” Dumont told his wife on the phone.
“That’s a young man who, if they don’t take action with him, is going to die in here,” said Cervelo Trujillo about Sendra Gonzalez.
Nobody has come by today, and we don’t know why,” Cervelo Trujillo told his wife over the phone.
text:
Despite the public demands of immigrant rights advocates for more than a year and the more recent pleas from families of those detained, the conditions at the Federal Detention Center in downtown Miami have not improved for detainees inside a facility designed for criminal felons — not suspected undocumented immigrants.

Weeks after Judith Castellanos, Anisley Cortes and Annett Uset-Dumont spoke out against what they called the ‘inhumane’ treatment of their husbands inside FDC at a press conference and called for the support of elected officials, they are frustrated and devastated at a complete lack of action. No elected official has inspected the facility since the press conference.

And since telling the media of FDC’s horrific conditions, the women have shared their recorded telephone conversations with WLRN to cast a critical spotlight on the facility housing hundreds of people accused of being in the country illegally.

One husband with diabetes spoke about being denied medical attention. Another told his wife of the sweltering heat and lack of air conditioning. The other told his spouse that cells got flooded with water forcing detainees to be moved to other parts of the facility.

The three women said they are speaking out because their husbands cannot while in detention.

“I’m going to be your voice at all times, and everyone is going to find out about all the injustices they’re committing against you,” Castellanos promised her husband.

The three women have been sharing her husband’s stories since they were relocated from Krome Detention Center to FDC in June.

“Animals get treated better than this,” Cervelo Trujillo told Castellanos over the phone. “We can’t go on like this.”

Cervelo Trujillo was detained at a routine immigration appointment at Krome North Service Processing Center in January and remained there until brushfires in June forced immigration officials to move him and dozens of other detainees to FDC in June. He emigrated from Cuba in 2005, and had applied for a green card within the last year.

The conditions described by current detainees at the FDC mirror the allegations and claims in a blistering Human Rights Watch report published almost a year ago to the day. In the July 2025 report, researchers interviewed hundreds of detainees at three South Florida facilities: Krome, FDC and the Broward Transitional Center.

The report, jointly produced by Human Rights Watch, Americans for Immigrant Justice and Sanctuary of the South, found the people locked up in the three South Florida immigration facilities were living under "abusive, degrading, and in some cases life-threatening" detention.

The FDC is a federal prison that holds those convicted of crimes in federal court. It began housing hundreds of suspected undocumented immigrants in February 2025 to accommodate the large number being apprehended by ICE agents under President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement strategy.

Human Rights Watch researchers say that conditions at FDC, Krome and BTC “violate international law and appear to violate key federal government standards as well.”

“ICE’s own detention standards require humane treatment, access to medical care, and protection from abuse,” the researchers wrote. “… ICE and its contractors are failing to meet these obligations.”

The wives of three detainees say their husbands have told them of inhumane living conditions, including broken or inadequate air conditioning in peak summer heat, cockroaches in the kitchen, undercooked, inedible food and toilets that did not flush.

READ MORE: Rights groups: 'Abusive, degrading' conditions exist at South Florida immigrant detention centers

Trapped in a ‘horrible stench’

From July 24 to July 27, Marlon Cervelo Trujillo had been in lockdown alongside every other detainee in FDC. He says the guards would not let the detainees leave their cells to shower, and their cell toilet had issues flushing for weeks.

He said the guards had told the detainees that the facility was locked down due to a ‘broken elevator.’ They only left their rooms to eat at mealtime. Otherwise, they were stuck in their cells, confined to the inhumane, miserable conditions at the prison.

“We’re stuck in here. The only time [the guards] open up is to hand out the food, and then they automatically lock up the door again,” Cervelo Trujillo told his Castellanos during the lockdown. “They’re not even taking us out to shower.”

A spokesperson with Immigration and Customs and Enforcement said that because the facility was operated by the Bureau of Prisons, they were unable to comment on the conditions inside.

A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson said that they could not comment on matters relating to immigrant detentions, and referred WLRN back to ICE media officials. The BOP spokesperson did say issues with the air conditioning and water were quickly resolved earlier this month.

BOP said that the organization does not comment on ‘anecdotal incidents.’

Coupled with the lack of the boiling temperature of the facility, Cervelo Trujillo says that the lockdown trapped detainees in a stinking hell. He said that the smell of weeks-old unflushed waste was inescapable.

“They haven’t fixed the toilets,” Cervelo Trujillo said. “This horrible stench of piss seeps out from under the doors, because there’s piss, there’s shit inside, and the toilets are still left like that.”

According to BOP, FDC Miami experienced an issue with water pressure at the facility in early July, but said that the issue was resolved the following day.

A BOP spokesperson told WLRN that, “inmates were provided additional bottles of water” during the incident and that, “during the short low-pressure period, inmates maintained access to ample amounts of potable water and the ability to flush toilets.”

Detainees claim the toilet issue has been ongoing since June, and that it has not yet been fixed.

The heat is ‘torture’

During their time at FDC, Cervelo Trujillo and Daikel Dumont — the spouse of Annett Uset-Dumont —both complained to their families about other unresolved issues regarding the air conditioning and rotten, roach-infested food as well.

Dumont, a Cuban man who has lived in the U.S. for 16 years, was detained at his home in front of his wife and their child, who was three at the time. He has since spent over eight months in detention: five months at Alligator Alcatraz and three at FDC Miami.

Dumont told his wife that he served food at FDC, and saw cockroaches in the supply earlier this month. He mentioned that the food was poor quality and borderline inedible.

“I saw the cockroach on the cart where the food comes in,” Dumont told his wife on the phone. “The food isn’t any good either, it’s a joke. What they bring you here and give you is nothing but pure junk.”

Cervelo Trujillo also agreed that the food they were given was ‘inedible.’

“They brought hamburgers, and honestly the meat looked like it was raw. It even smelled bad,” said Cervelo Trujillo.

BOP has not commented on any allegations made about the quality of food inside the facility.

A BOP spokesperson did tell WLRN that there was a malfunction with one of the air conditioning’s chillers earlier this month that was quickly resolved.

“The facilities department immediately identified the issue and began repairs… both chillers are operating as intended and as they were before the identified malfunction,” a BOP spokesperson said. “During the outage, staff and inmates had access to alternative means of remaining cool, such as ceiling fans or industrial fans.”

Dumont said that he could not feel air conditioning in his cell, and that the facility’s industrial fans were no match for the heat.

“This is basically torture, because you're up almost six hours, just lying there on a piece of cardboard because the heat is suffocating,” Dumont told his wife. “We have one fan for the eighty-two or ninety-two people who are in this room.”

READ MORE: Families, advocates protest 'inhumane' conditions at downtown Miami Federal Detention Center

Dumont was transferred to Krome Detention Center last week, where he worked as a barber, according to his wife. She says his living conditions at Krome are better than what he experienced at FDC.

Medical neglect

In their calls to their wives, Dumont and Cervelo Trujillo often mentioned the inadequate medical care in the facility. They both recalled the unit only having one nurse, who would often refuse patients at night.

“The only time they’ll see you at night is if you’re really serious, otherwise they won’t treat you,” Dumont told his wife. “They say ICE didn’t send our medical records over here, or our medications. That’s their justification.”

Dumont has chronic asthma, which he told his wife he was struggling with in mid July after the guards had pepper sprayed several detainees. Cervelo Trujillo has high blood pressure as a long-term complication of COVID-19, which his wife often worries about.

Both men’s primary concern, though, was a detainee named Noslen Sendra Gonzalez. He consistently had medical issues that staff ignored, until his health became so poor that he was transferred to a different facility.

“That’s a young man who, if they don’t take action with him, is going to die in here,” said Cervelo Trujillo about Sendra Gonzalez.

Sendra Gonzalez, a Cuban immigrant from Orlando, was first detained during a routine immigration appointment in November. He was placed in Krome Detention Center, and after the brush fires in June, was moved to FDC.

Sendra Gonzalez has Type 2 Diabetes and requires access to insulin, which he and other detainees alleged inadequate and infrequent access to.

His wife, Anisley Cortes, warned FDC officials about his condition weeks before he had a medical emergency. She said her husband was previously hospitalized once for high triglycerides and twice for pancreatitis.

“It’s a critical situation. If he gets pancreatitis again he could die there,” Cortes said at a press conference a few weeks prior. “All I ask is that he is given medical attention.”

In FDC, Sendra Gonzalez had extremely high triglycerides and worsening pancreatitis. His condition was deemed to be so poor that he was moved out of the facility.

On July 22, he was transferred to Krome to receive better medical treatment. His wife said that he has been in the hospital there for over a week.

Flooded cells

A week after Dumont and Sendra Gonzalez were transferred, water began to drip into the cells of several detainees. Cervelo Trujillo, who is still detained at FDC, said that on July 29 the water flooded the floors and soaked the mattresses of at least two rooms, and the hallway outside was filled with water.

He helped a few detainees move to rooms that were not flooded. The guards had not helped the detainees, who were left to sleep on soaking wet mattresses, and for several hours after, the water was not cleaned up, he said.

“It’s completely flooded. Nobody has come by today, and we don’t know why,” Cervelo Trujillo told his wife over the phone.

The Bureau of Prisons did not respond to this claim in time for publication.

He says that between the stagnant water, detainees spitting on the ground and the cockroaches escaping to dry floors, he is worried that they might all start getting sick.

text:
It didn’t take Eva Saltzman very long to pack up a decade’s worth of material from her tenure as an immigration judge.

Less than 24 hours after she received an emailed termination notice in the middle of a hearing, Saltzman stood with a carful of office supplies, art and certificates, trying to think through the fact that her time on the bench had come to an end.

She is one of two judges fired Thursday from Chicago’s Immigration Court, which has seen seismic changes since President Donald Trump returned to office. The local court has recently become the national leader in deportation orders.

Saltzman had been with the court since 2016; one of the items she brought home Friday was the framed certification bearing then-Attorney General Loretta Lynch’s signature. The second judge fired Thursday, Elizabeth Crites, had been there since 2021.

According to the National Association of Immigration Judges, another judge was fired in June, continuing a wave of firings, resignations and buyouts from the Chicago bench as Trump, who has direct oversight of the country’s immigration courts, seeks to reshape them in the image of his hard-line agenda.

Advocates, attorneys and ex-judges all say the changing lineup on the immigration bench, combined with changes to many of the basic elements that define the life of an immigration case, have all helped transform Chicago’s court into the national epicenter of removal orders: from issuing 35 a day on average during President Joe Biden’s final year in office to more than 125 a day this year.

Jeremiah Johnson, the executive vice president of the National Association of Immigration Judges and himself a recently terminated judge, referred to the exodus as a “purge” and added in a message to the Tribune that the firing of “experienced immigration judges without cause is another example of the attack on the independence of our immigration courts.”

A representative with the Executive Office for Immigration Review, which runs the country’s immigration courts as part of the U.S. Department of Justice, said the office didn’t comment on personnel matters.

Crites, reached by phone, confirmed she’d been fired but made no other comment.

Saltzman, for her part, said she had been stunned by the firing, but not necessarily surprised.

“I’ve served as an immigration judge for the last decade, and, under this administration, I continued to do my job the way I’ve always done it, giving careful consideration to each case and applying the law to each case,” she said. “And I’ve long anticipated that under this administration, performing my duties in this way may result in my termination.”

That said, she continued, there had been no immediate warning signs that she was about to be terminated.

On Friday morning, outside the Loop high-rise that’s home to most of Chicago’s immigration proceedings, Saltzman thought about what the rest of the day might look like. She’d have dinner with one of her daughters and some friends, she said. There would be more time to train for an open-water sprint triathlon, the first she’s attempted.

Saltzman’s time with the court coincided with explosive growth in the country’s national immigration caseload. But over the last few months, the court in some ways became busier still as Trump administration officials pushed to cut down a case backlog still topping 3 million, per the immigration data clearinghouse TRAC.

The Tribune reported earlier this month how Chicago’s immigration court had become the national epicenter of removal orders across the country, using Department of Justice data — obtained and refined by the research group Deportation Data Project — to find that even Biden-era judges saw notable swings toward issuing higher rates of removal orders once Trump took office.

That was true of Judges Crites and Saltzman as well, but the Tribune analysis found that they still lagged their peers’ prolific pace of removal orders.

When looking at all judges who concluded at least 50 cases that month — and excluding cases that ended with the immigrant voluntarily deciding to leave — the analysis found these two judges had the two lowest percentages of cases concluding in the issuance of removal orders. Crites handled the court’s juvenile cases, while Saltzman was one of two judges hearing cases from the detained docket, for people who are fighting their cases while in Department of Homeland Security custody.

For Judge Crites, the analysis found that she concluded roughly a fifth of her more than 500 June cases by dismissing, terminating or otherwise closing them without issuing a removal order — the kind of nuanced ending that can frustrate those pushing for mass deportation.

Judge Saltzman issued the fewest removal orders in the group, just 33 in an immigration courthouse where judges typically issued hundreds that month and where one judge issued more than 900. Saltzman said Thursday these findings weren’t surprising to her at all, given the caseload she worked with.

Immigrants who choose to fight to stay in the U.S. from detention tend to do so because their cases stand a good chance of getting a favorable outcome, she said: “The relief applications that I am considering are self-selected in a way that makes them more likely to be cases that should be granted.”

The other consequence of Saltzman’s hearing the detained docket was that her caseload drew a substantial amount of media attention, most recently in the case of Reuben Torres Maldonado. Torres Maldonado’s 16-year-old daughter, Ofelia Torres, was in the throes of treatment for Stage 4 cancer when federal agents arrested him at the height of Operation Midway Blitz. Ofelia Torres died in February.

Saltzman, as she made the decision to release him on bond Oct. 30, noted he is an unlikely flight risk and has a case to potentially remain in the United States.

“I wish you much luck in the future and I wish your daughter a full recovery,” she said.

While her docket tended to attract higher-profile cases like that of the Torres family, Saltzman said she’d “never made a decision with any particular agenda or end goal in mind.”

Chicago Tribune’s Joe Mahr contributed.
